High Rank and Multiplicity in Random and Perfect Profinite Groups

Carlo Pagano ††thanks: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Concordia University, Quebec H3G 1M8, Canada, carlein90@gmail.com; Google DeepMind, carlopagano@google.com. Affiliation: Concordia University and Google DeepMind    Mark Shusterman ††thanks: The Dr. A. Edward Friedmann Career Development Chair in Mathematics at the Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Weizmann Institute of Science, 234 Herzl Street, Rehovot 76100, Israel. Affiliation: Weizmann Institute of Science
September 24, 2026
Abstract

We prove that almost sure topological finite generation holds for a general class of random models of profinite groups. We deduce that in the models introduced by Liu–Wood and Sawin–Wood, one has that finite presentation holds almost surely, with almost sure control of the deficiency in the presentation. In particular this settles questions raised in [22] and [30].

Using the same underlying principle, we show that there exists a unique universal dd-generated perfect profinite group: its finite quotients are precisely the finite dd-generated perfect groups. This settles Conjecture B1 posed by Nikolov in [25]. We show in addition that this group is projective and admits a profinite presentation with dd generators and dd relations, and with no fewer relations on dd generators.

The main underlying theme is to bring in an insight from crown theory: groups with high rank are always witnessed by a crown with large multiplicity.

This approach was discovered independently by ChatGPT5.5 pro and Aletheia, an internal agent at Google DeepMind.

1 Introduction

The rich web of analogies and dictionaries between number fields, algebraic curves and 33-manifolds is pervasive in modern number theory. Recently, these dictionaries have found particularly fertile grounds in the context of random profinite group models and their applications to arithmetic statistics, in a remarkable series of works of Sawin–Wood [30, 28, 29], building on previous work of Liu–Wood [22] and Liu–Wood–Zureick-Brown [23]. Such random groups are used to provide heuristic models for the étale fundamental group π1ét​(Spec​(𝒪K))\pi_{1}^{\text{ét}}(\text{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{K})) when KK varies in natural families of number fields. Grounding evidence for these heuristics can be provided for curves over finite fields, thanks to the groundbreaking work of Ellenberg–Venkatesh–Westerland [8] and the recent breakthrough of Landesmann–Levy [15, 16]. The dependency of these heuristics on the base field leads to a plethora of random group models. It is precisely exploring the analogy with 33-manifolds that, in the hands of Sawin–Wood [30, 29], the literature has arrived at a convincing model for completely general base number/function fields.

Despite the compelling evidence over function fields, very little is known about π1ét​(Spec​(𝒪K))\pi_{1}^{\text{\'{e}t}}(\text{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{K})), when KK is a number field. A difficult conjecture of Shafarevich [31, p. 167], also motivated by the analogy with algebraic curves, postulates that this is a topologically finitely generated group. Hence it is a natural question whether the random group models produce finitely generated groups almost surely. This question has been raised by Liu–Wood [22] and by Sawin–Wood [30] for their respective models, as we shall recall more precisely below.

Our first main result settles both cases. With an eye towards future applications, we provide a general statement that can be applied to any random group model as soon as it satisfies a certain growth condition for its so-called moments. A moment is the average value of |Epitop.gr.​(𝒢,H)||\text{Epi}_{\text{top.gr.}}(\mathcal{G},H)|, where HH is any given finite group. One of the key insights, ubiquitous in many works in this area and championed in [30, 28], is that these moments provide a systematic way to study our random group model (and they are often sufficiently powerful to encode the whole distribution).

Let (Ω,ℬ,μ)(\Omega,\mathcal{B},\mu) be a probability space whose points are profinite groups and such that the functions 𝒢↦|Epitop.gr.​(𝒢,H)|\mathcal{G}\mapsto|\text{Epi}_{\text{top.gr.}}(\mathcal{G},H)| are measurable and there exist constants α,δ≥0\alpha,\delta\geq 0 with

supH1|H|α⋅|H2​(H,ℤ)|δ​∫Ω|Epitop.gr.​(𝒢,H)|​𝑑μ<∞,\sup_{H}\frac{1}{|H|^{\alpha}\cdot|H_{2}(H,\mathbb{Z})|^{\delta}}\int_{\Omega}|\text{Epi}_{\text{top.gr.}}(\mathcal{G},H)|\,d\mu<\infty,

where HH ranges over all finite groups. We call such a space a decent space of random groups. For a profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we denote by d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) the infimum among all of the cardinals of the subsets of 𝒢\mathcal{G} that are topologically generating 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Theorem 1.1.

Let (Ω,ℬ,μ)(\Omega,\mathcal{B},\mu) be a decent space of profinite groups. Then the set {𝒢∈Ω:d⁡(𝒢)<∞}\{\mathcal{G}\in\Omega:d(\mathcal{G})<\infty\} is measurable, i.e. it is an element of ℬ\mathcal{B}, and furthermore

μ⁡({𝒢∈Ω:d⁡(𝒢)<∞})=1,\mu(\{\mathcal{G}\in\Omega:d(\mathcal{G})<\infty\})=1,

that is, an element 𝒢\mathcal{G} of Ω\Omega is topologically finitely generated almost surely.

Theorem 1.1 has a much more precise incarnation in the context of [22, 30]. To explain that, we briefly recall how these random models are constructed.

Let F^n\widehat{F}_{n} denote the free profinite group on nn generators. For an integer uu and n+u≥0n+u\geq 0, Liu and Wood [22] consider

Xu,n=F^n/⟨r1,…,rn+u⟩¯,X_{u,n}=\widehat{F}_{n}/\overline{\langle r_{1},\ldots,r_{n+u}\rangle},

where the rir_{i} are independent Haar-random elements of F^n\widehat{F}_{n}. As n→∞n\to\infty, these groups converge in law to a measure μu\mu_{u} on a natural probability space 𝒫\mathcal{P} of profinite groups. We write XuX_{u} for a random profinite group with law μu\mu_{u}.

On the topological side, Dunfield and Thurston [7] considered a random closed oriented 33-manifold Mg,LM_{g,L} by gluing two genus-gg handlebodies with a random word of length LL in the mapping class group. Sawin and Wood prove that, first as L→∞L\to\infty and then as g→∞g\to\infty, the groups π1​(Mg,L)^\widehat{\pi_{1}(M_{g,L})} converge to a random group picked by a probability measure μSW\mu_{\mathrm{SW}} introduced in [30]. At finite level Xu,nX_{u,n} has nn generators and n+un+u random relations, whereas a genus-gg Heegaard splitting gives gg generators and gg relations. Remarkably, this pattern propagates at the infinite level, as our next two results show.

Recall that Liu and Wood asked whether their limiting groups are nevertheless finitely generated and finitely presented [22, p.3]; Sawin and Wood asked whether their limiting group is topologically finitely generated [30, Section 10.3].

It is now an immediate consequence of Theorem 1.1 that both XuX_{u} and a μSW\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}-random group are topologically finitely generated almost surely. The next two results say that the same holds for finite presentation and, furthermore, the presentation shape used to construct the groups at finite level propagates at infinite level.

Theorem 1.2.

The locus in 𝒫\mathcal{P} of groups 𝒢\mathcal{G} admitting a profinite presentation with d:=d⁡(𝒢)<∞d:=d(\mathcal{G})<\infty generators and dd relations, and admitting no profinite presentation with fewer than dd relations, is Borel. For μSW\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}-almost every 𝒢∈𝒫\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{P} the quantity dd is finite and there exist x1,…,xd∈F^dx_{1},\ldots,x_{d}\in\widehat{F}_{d} such that

𝒢∼top.gr.F^d/⟨x1,…,xd⟩¯.\mathcal{G}{\sim}_{\textup{top.gr.}}\widehat{F}_{d}/\overline{\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}\rangle}.

Moreover, almost surely every finite profinite presentation of 𝒢\mathcal{G} with nn generators and rr relations satisfies r≥n≥dr\geq n\geq d. Thus the minimum numbers of generators and relations are both dd. In particular, a Sawin–Wood random group is topologically finitely presented with probability 11.

Theorem 1.2 settles in particular Sawin–Wood’s question in a strong form.

We next turn to the Liu–Wood model, with the following result.

Theorem 1.3.

The locus of finitely presented groups is Borel in the Liu–Wood space 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Moreover, for every u∈ℤu\in\mathbb{Z} and for μu\mu_{u}-almost every 𝒢∈𝒫\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{P}, the integer d=d⁡(𝒢)d=d(\mathcal{G}) is finite, one has that d>−ud>-u if u<0u<0, and there exist x1,…,xd+u∈F^dx_{1},\ldots,x_{d+u}\in\widehat{F}_{d} such that

𝒢≅F^d/⟨x1,…,xd+u⟩¯.\mathcal{G}\cong\widehat{F}_{d}/\overline{\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{d+u}\rangle}.

In particular, XuX_{u} is topologically finitely presented with probability 11.

The underlying principle of the proof can be used to settle a conjecture of Nikolov: he conjectured that, for each d>1d>1, there exists a topologically finitely generated perfect profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G} that has every finite perfect dd-generated group among its quotients [25, Conjecture B1]. Our next result proves a slightly stronger statement.

Theorem 1.4.

Let dd be an integer at least 22. Then there is a topologically dd-generated profinite group UdU_{d} such that

Ud=[Ud,Ud]U_{d}=[U_{d},U_{d}]

as an abstract group and every finite perfect group HH with d⁡(H)≤dd(H)\leq d is a continuous quotient of UdU_{d}. Furthermore UdU_{d} is unique up to isomorphism, it is projective and admits a profinite presentation with dd generators and dd relations; no profinite presentation of UdU_{d} has fewer than dd relations.

1.1 Method of proof

We first describe the main ideas behind the proof of Theorem 1.1.

An initial observation dating back to Cohen–Lenstra [1], i.e. the very source of random group theory applied to number theory, is that highly symmetric objects should occur rarely. A simple example of a finite group with high rank is 𝔽pn\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}, i.e. a group which has a high multiplicity, which translates into a massive group of symmetries. At the same time for an abelian (or even pro-nilpotent) 𝒢\mathcal{G} one would be able to witness the event d⁡(𝒢)>md(\mathcal{G})>m via the events 𝒢↠𝔽pm+1\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m+1} and the general Cohen–Lenstra-principle incarnates into the inequality

μ⁡(𝒢↠H)≪|H|α⋅|H2​(H,ℤ)|δ|Autgr​(H)|,\mu(\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow H)\ll\frac{|H|^{\alpha}\cdot|H_{2}(H,\mathbb{Z})|^{\delta}}{|\text{Aut}_{\text{gr}}(H)|}, (1)

for each finite group HH. Before discussing how one actually capitalizes from this (we still need to sum over all primes pp), we first need to explain how we face the more fundamental task: namely to find a non-abelian generalization of this picture. We use the following principle from crown theory. This theory provides a list of atomic groups called monoliths and a notion of crown power of a monolith. Before describing these notions, we give the principle.

Principle: Finite groups with large rank are always witnessed by a large crown power of a monolith.

To make this principle precise, we remark that the example 𝔽pn⋊𝔽p∗\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}\rtimes\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*} shows very clearly that a group might manifest no multiplicity at all, 11 1 in the sense of surjecting on some group of the form HNH^{N} for some large NN. but have still high rank, hence the need for a subtler notion of power. In the language of crown theory, in this example the crown multiplicity is in fact nn and this is the crown power of the monolith 𝔽p⋊𝔽p∗\mathbb{F}_{p}\rtimes\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}. Monoliths come in two flavors: of abelian type and of non-abelian type. The ones of abelian type are a straightforward generalization of the example 𝔽p⋊𝔽p∗\mathbb{F}_{p}\rtimes\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}: namely these are the groups of the form V⋊KV\rtimes K, where VV is an irreducible faithful representation of KK over a prime field. The nn-th crown power of this is Vn⋊KV^{n}\rtimes K.

The deep works of Gaschütz–Lucchini [11, 4, 18], Guralnick–Hoffman [12] and Lucchini–Thakkar [19] provide a powerful generalization of the abelian case: for m≥2m\geq 2 the event {d(𝒢)>m}\{d(\mathcal{G})>m\} is always witnessed by 𝒢\mathcal{G} surjecting to the fL​(m)f_{L}(m)-th crown power where fL​(m)f_{L}(m) is a function of mm that depends on the monolith LL in an explicit fashion.

Without a sufficiently good control on fL​(m)f_{L}(m) simply listing all of the monoliths (e.g. listing all of relevant KK’s above inside OPENAut​(V))\text{Aut}(V))) would defeat the gain obtained from large automorphisms and make the bound one gets from equation (1) vacuous. That control is provided in the abelian case by Guralnick–Hoffman and in the non-abelian case by Lucchini–Thakkar. Injecting these results into (1) and capitalizing on the obvious automorphisms coming from large multiplicity yields Theorem 1.1 upon summing the contributions along all monoliths. A slightly subtler detail here is that at the phase transition δ=2\delta=2 one needs to switch from automorphisms of a large crown power to surjections of a large crown power to a smaller one and a corresponding version of equation (1). We emphasize that this part of the proof, devoted to control the quantity fL​(m)f_{L}(m), relies indirectly, yet heavily, on the classification of finite simple groups, as the currently known proofs of these results rely on that.

To pass from Theorem 1.1 to Theorem 1.2, we use the criterion of Sawin–Wood [30, Theorem 1.5] and a relation-module argument giving dd generators and at most dd relations [20, Theorems 3.1 and 5.1]. The opposite inequality comes from the fact that the maximal abelian pro-22 quotient is finite almost surely: a presentation with nn generators and rr relations gives a quotient of ℤ2n\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{n} by rr vectors, and finiteness forces r≥nr\geq n. For Theorem 1.3, convergence of the finite Liu–Wood models supplies presentations in each finite pro-SS-category. A relation-module argument reduces the number of generators while preserving the difference between the numbers of relations and generators [22, Lemma 13.1]. This reduction requires at least one relator; for u<0u<0, we prove that d⁡(𝒢)>−ud(\mathcal{G})>-u almost surely, which supplies this condition. A compactness argument then gives the global presentation.

Finally in the proof of Theorem 1.4 we run the principle above in the opposite direction. The group we build must cover every finite perfect dd-generated group, so it contains chief series of unbounded length, and the whole point is to stack these chief factors so that no monolith LL reaches crown multiplicity fL​(d)f_{L}(d), the critical multiplicity at which the rank would exceed dd. This process happens in Lemma 7.3 and we explain it in a self-contained manner, however the steps in the proof naturally stem out of crown theory and we expand that in Remark 7.5.

1.2 Further results

For the Liu–Wood measure we can go beyond almost surely finite generation and provide precise asymptotic control on the distribution of 𝒢↦d⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{G}\mapsto d(\mathcal{G}).

Theorem 1.5.

For every fixed u∈ℤu\in\mathbb{Z},

μu​{𝒢∈𝒫:d⁡(𝒢)=r}∼2−r⁡(r+u)∏j=1∞(1−2−j)(r→∞).\mu_{u}\{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{P}:d(\mathcal{G})=r\}\sim\frac{2^{-r(r+u)}}{\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{\infty}(1-2^{-j})}\qquad(r\to\infty).

More precisely, if ηq​(k)=∏j=1k(1−q−j)\eta_{q}(k)=\prod_{j=1}^{k}(1-q^{-j}) and ηq​(∞)=∏j≥1(1−q−j)\eta_{q}(\infty)=\prod_{j\geq 1}(1-q^{-j}), then

μu​{𝒢∈𝒫:d⁡(𝒢)=r}=η2​(∞)η2​(r)​η2​(r+u)​2−r⁡(r+u)+Ou​(3−r2+Cu​r)\mu_{u}\{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{P}:d(\mathcal{G})=r\}=\frac{\eta_{2}(\infty)}{\eta_{2}(r)\eta_{2}(r+u)}2^{-r(r+u)}+O_{u}\bigl(3^{-r^{2}+C_{u}r}\bigr)

for all sufficiently large rr, where CuC_{u} depends only on uu.

Theorem 1.5 can be interpreted as saying that the crown powers of the monolith 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} are asymptotically capturing the behavior of the function d⁡(−)d(-). In fact, we believe that Theorem 1.5 is only the first order approximation of the full story. There should be a full asymptotic expansion labeled by monoliths suitably ordered each coming at the appropriate time with an explicit term. It would be very interesting to explore this story in full.

Recall that a profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G} is positively finitely generated (PFG) if, for some integer d≥1d\geq 1, the tuples that generate 𝒢\mathcal{G} topologically form a subset of positive Haar measure in 𝒢d\mathcal{G}^{d} [24]. It has uniformly bounded exponential representation growth (UBERG) if there exists a constant c>0c>0 such that, for every prime pp and every integer n≥1n\geq 1, the number of isomorphism classes of continuous irreducible nn-dimensional representations of 𝒢\mathcal{G} over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} is at most pc​np^{cn} [14, Definition 5.1]. Positive finite generation implies UBERG [3, Corollary 1.11]. Our next result determines exactly when these properties hold in the Liu–Wood model.

Theorem 1.6.

Let u∈ℤu\in\mathbb{Z}, and let 𝒢\mathcal{G} have law μu\mu_{u}. If u≥−1u\geq-1, then almost surely 𝒢\mathcal{G} is PFG and has UBERG. If u≤−2u\leq-2, then almost surely 𝒢\mathcal{G} is not PFG and does not have UBERG.

See Theorem 8.4 for a complete and slightly more refined statement, controlling some crown multiplicities of non-abelian types almost surely.

Finally, we remark that the original random group model introduced in Liu–Wood [22] needs to accomodate extra-structure when one considers families of Γ\Gamma-extensions of ℚ\mathbb{Q}, mostly coming from the Γ\Gamma-action, as carried out by Liu–Wood–Zureick-Brown [23]. One can see that Theorem 1.1 applies easily to that case. This is done in Section 8.1.

1.3 Layout of the paper

Section 2 develops the basics and the notion of mm-witnesses. Section 3 implements crown theory and gives a very efficient set of mm-witnesses. Section 4 carries out the resulting estimates, proves Theorem 1.1, and applies it to both the limiting Liu–Wood and Sawin–Wood measures. Section 5 proves Theorems 1.2 and 1.3. Section 6 proves Theorem 1.5. Section 7 proves Theorem 1.4, that is Nikolov’s Conjecture B1, together with the uniqueness, projectivity and presentation statements. Section 8 proves Theorem 1.6 and gives further applications of Theorem 1.1.

1.4 Human–AI collaboration

The idea of using crown theory to transfer high generator rank into a high automorphism cost was discovered first by GPT5.5 pro in two separate conversations with the authors (respectively about the solvable regime, i.e. abelian type crowns, and non-solvable regime, i.e. non-abelian type crowns). The entire proof of Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 was subsequently and independently discovered also by Aletheia [9], an internal agent at Google DeepMind. Autonomous proofs of Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 were also obtained using Google’s Colosseum harness [17] and Cogentic framework from Google Research.

While digesting the ideas of the proof, the authors have then explored natural further directions and applications, which culminated in the other results presented above. This exploration has been done in a collaborative fashion with GPT5.6 Sol pro, Fable as well as with internal agents at Google DeepMind. We now explain this exploration in greater detail, outlining what happened for each of the other results:

  1. 1.

    Theorem 1.2, Theorem 1.5 and Theorem 1.6 were discovered by the authors.

  2. 2.

    Theorem 1.4 was discovered as follows. The authors wanted to explore to what extent Theorem 1.1 could be used from the viewpoint of the probabilistic method to construct interesting profinite groups. They prompted AI-agents from all the models above to explore possibilities. After scanning a long list of possible applications provided by AI, the authors selected to explore Conjecture B1 of Nikolov, where GPT5.6 Sol pro discovered a proof.

Once the process above settled, the authors have used Astra to draft this work in a back-and-forth fashion as follows. The first version was produced by AI following the authors’ instructions. They then rewrote, or in some places asked Astra to rewrite, or occasionally both, the entirety of the text, which was subsequently proofread (by both the authors and Astra) and edited several times until it reached a status that satisfied them.

2 mm-witnesses

For a profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, let d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) denote the least cardinality of a finite topological generating set, with d⁡(𝒢)=∞d(\mathcal{G})=\infty if no such set exists. All epimorphisms from profinite groups to finite groups will be understood to be continuous.

Definition 2.1.

Let (Ω,ℬ,μ)(\Omega,\mathcal{B},\mu) be a probability space whose points are profinite groups up to isomorphism. For every finite group HH, set

νH​(𝒢)=|Sur⁡(𝒢,H)|∈ℤ≥0∪{∞},\nu_{H}(\mathcal{G})=|\Sur(\mathcal{G},H)|\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\cup\{\infty\},

where any infinite cardinality is recorded as ∞\infty. We say that (Ω,ℬ,μ)(\Omega,\mathcal{B},\mu) is decent if νH\nu_{H} is measurable for every finite group HH and if there are fixed constants M≥1M\geq 1 and α,δ≥0\alpha,\delta\geq 0 such that for all finite groups HH

∫νH​(𝒢)​𝑑μ≤M​|H|α​|H2​(H,ℤ)|δ.\int\nu_{H}(\mathcal{G})d\mu\leq M|H|^{\alpha}|H_{2}(H,\mathbb{Z})|^{\delta}. (2)
Remark 2.2.

For a finite group HH, the event

E⁡(H):={𝒢∈Ω:𝒢↠H}={𝒢∈Ω:νH​(𝒢)>0}E(H):=\{\mathcal{G}\in\Omega:\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow H\}=\{\mathcal{G}\in\Omega:\nu_{H}(\mathcal{G})>0\}

is measurable in every decent probability space. Moreover, postcomposition defines a free action of Aut​(H)\text{Aut}(H) on Sur​(𝒢,H)\text{Sur}(\mathcal{G},H). Consequently,

𝟏E⁡(H)​(𝒢)≤νH​(𝒢)|Aut⁡(H)|.\mathbf{1}_{E(H)}(\mathcal{G})\leq\frac{\nu_{H}(\mathcal{G})}{|\Aut(H)|}.

In particular, in a decent probability space

μ⁡(E⁡(H))≤𝔼μ​[νH]|Aut⁡(H)|≤M⋅|H|α⋅|H2​(H,ℤ)|δ|Aut⁡(H)|.\mu(E(H))\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\nu_{H}]}{|\Aut(H)|}\leq M\cdot\frac{|H|^{\alpha}\cdot|H_{2}(H,\mathbb{Z})|^{\delta}}{|\Aut(H)|}. (3)
Proposition 2.3.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a profinite group and let m≥0m\geq 0 be an integer. Then d⁡(𝒢)>md(\mathcal{G})>m if and only if 𝒢\mathcal{G} has a finite continuous quotient HH such that d⁡(H)>md(H)>m.

Proof.

One implication is immediate, since the image of a topologically generating set generates every finite continuous quotient. For the converse one has merely to select in a compatible fashion a set of generators of size mm among the ones available at every finite level. This follows at once from the fact that an inverse limit of finite non-empty sets is itself non-empty, which can be easily seen by a compactness argument. ∎

For m≥0m\geq 0, write

Em:={𝒢∈Ω:d⁡(𝒢)>m}.E_{m}:=\{\mathcal{G}\in\Omega:d(\mathcal{G})>m\}.
Proposition 2.4.

If (Ω,ℬ,μ)(\Omega,\mathcal{B},\mu) is decent, then EmE_{m} is measurable.

Proof.

There are only countably many isomorphism classes of finite groups of rank bigger than mm and Proposition 2.3 gives

Em=⋃H:d⁡(H)>mE(H).E_{m}=\bigcup_{H:d(H)>m}E(H).

Each event on the right is measurable by Remark 2.2, so EmE_{m} is measurable. ∎

Proposition 2.3 suggests detecting EmE_{m} using a smaller collection of carefully chosen finite quotients.

Definition 2.5.

A countable collection {Hi}i∈I\{H_{i}\}_{i\in I} of finite groups is a set of mm-witnesses if, for every profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G},

d(𝒢)>m⟺𝒢↠Hi for some i∈I.d(\mathcal{G})>m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow H_{i}\text{ for some }i\in I.

Equivalently, in every probability space of profinite groups,

Em=⋃i∈IE⁡(Hi).E_{m}=\bigcup_{i\in I}E(H_{i}).

For every finite group HH, the event E⁡(H)E(H) occurring here is measurable in every decent probability space by Remark 2.2.

Proposition 2.6.

Let {Hi}i∈I\{H_{i}\}_{i\in I} be a set of mm-witnesses, and let (Ω,ℬ,μ)(\Omega,\mathcal{B},\mu) be a decent probability space of profinite groups. Then

μ⁡(Em)≤∑i∈Iμ⁡(E⁡(Hi)).\mu(E_{m})\leq\sum_{i\in I}\mu(E(H_{i})).

If the space is decent with constants M,α,δM,\alpha,\delta, then

μ⁡(Em)≤M⋅∑i∈I|Hi|α⋅|H2​(Hi,ℤ)|δ|Aut⁡(Hi)|.\mu(E_{m})\leq M\cdot\sum_{i\in I}\frac{|H_{i}|^{\alpha}\cdot|H_{2}(H_{i},\mathbb{Z})|^{\delta}}{|\Aut(H_{i})|}. (4)
Proof.

The first assertion follows from Definition 2.5 and countable subadditivity. The second follows by applying (3) to each HiH_{i}. ∎

Remark 2.7.

Proposition 2.3 shows that the collection of all finite groups HH with d⁡(H)>md(H)>m, with one representative from each isomorphism class, is a set of mm-witnesses. Our next goal is to replace this collection by a substantially more efficient one for which the series in (4) can be estimated.

3 Crown theory

3.1 Abstract and concrete monoliths

Definition 3.1.

A finite group LL is monolithic if it has a unique minimal normal subgroup; this subgroup is denoted by A=soc⁡(L)A=\soc(L) and called the monolith of LL. The group is monolithic primitive if A≰Frat⁡(L)A\not\leq\Frat(L).

For t≥1t\geq 1, the tt-th crown-based power of a monolithic group LL is

Lt:={(ℓ1,…,ℓt)∈Lt:ℓ1A=⋯=ℓtA}=L×L/A⋯×L/AL.L_{t}:=\{(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{t})\in L^{t}:\ell_{1}A=\cdots=\ell_{t}A\}=L\times_{L/A}\cdots\times_{L/A}L.

Thus Lt/At≅L/AL_{t}/A^{t}\cong L/A, and projection onto any s≤ts\leq t coordinates is an epimorphism Lt↠LsL_{t}\twoheadrightarrow L_{s}.

Definition 3.2.

A concrete monolithic datum is one of the following.

  1. (A)

    A prime pp, a nonzero finite-dimensional 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-vector space VV, and a subgroup K≤GL⁡(V)K\leq\GL(V) acting faithfully and irreducibly. We put

    L=V⋊KL=V\rtimes K

    and call LL a monolithic group of abelian type. The case K=1K=1 forces V≅𝔽pV\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}.

  2. (B)

    A finite nonabelian simple group SS, an integer ρ≥1\rho\geq 1, and a subgroup

    K≤Out⁡(Sρ)≅Out⁡(S)≀SymρK\leq\Out(S^{\rho})\cong\Out(S)\wr\Sym_{\rho}

    whose permutation action on the ρ\rho simple factors is transitive. If

    π:Aut⁡(Sρ)↠Out⁡(Sρ)\pi:\Aut(S^{\rho})\twoheadrightarrow\Out(S^{\rho})

    is the quotient map, we put L=π−1​(K)L=\pi^{-1}(K) and call LL a monolithic group of nonabelian type.

We remark that in the nonabelian case the resulting group extension need not to be a split one.

Proposition 3.3.

A finite group is monolithic primitive if and only if it is isomorphic to a group arising from construction (A) or (B) in Definition 3.2.

Proof.

Let LL be monolithic primitive, with unique minimal normal subgroup AA.

Suppose first that AA is abelian. Then AA is elementary abelian. Since A≰Frat⁡(L)A\not\leq\Frat(L), there is a maximal subgroup UU of LL not containing AA. Thus L=A​UL=AU. The subgroup A∩UA\cap U is normalized by UU and centralized by AA, hence is normal in LL. Minimality of AA gives A∩U=1A\cap U=1, so L=A⋊UL=A\rtimes U. The action of UU on AA is irreducible by minimality of AA. Its kernel is normalized by UU and centralized by AA, hence is normal in LL. Since it intersects AA trivially, it must be trivial. Thus the action is faithful, giving construction (A).

Suppose now that AA is nonabelian. Then A≅SρA\cong S^{\rho} for a finite nonabelian simple group SS and an integer ρ≥1\rho\geq 1. The subgroup CL​(A)C_{L}(A) is normal in LL and satisfies CL​(A)∩A=Z⁡(A)=1C_{L}(A)\cap A=Z(A)=1, so CL​(A)=1C_{L}(A)=1. Conjugation therefore embeds LL in Aut⁡(A)\Aut(A), with AA identified with Inn⁡(A)\Inn(A). Since this image contains Inn⁡(A)\Inn(A), it is the full inverse image of a subgroup K≤Out⁡(A)K\leq\Out(A). The product of the simple factors in any KK-orbit is normal in LL, so minimality of AA forces this action to be transitive. This gives construction (B).

Conversely, let LL arise from either construction, and let AA denote VV in (A) and Inn⁡(Sρ)≅Sρ\Inn(S^{\rho})\cong S^{\rho} in (B). Irreducibility in (A) and transitivity in (B) show that AA is minimal normal in LL. Moreover, CL​(A)=AC_{L}(A)=A in (A) and CL​(A)=1C_{L}(A)=1 in (B). If N​⊴​LN\trianglelefteq L satisfies N∩A=1N\cap A=1, then [N,A]≤N∩A=1[N,A]\leq N\cap A=1; these centralizer identities therefore imply N=1N=1. Thus AA is the unique minimal normal subgroup.

In (A), a maximal subgroup containing the complement KK cannot contain AA, so A≰Frat⁡(L)A\not\leq\Frat(L). In (B), AA is not nilpotent, whereas Frat⁡(L)\Frat(L) is nilpotent, so again A≰Frat⁡(L)A\not\leq\Frat(L). Hence LL is monolithic primitive. ∎

The data in these two descriptions can be recovered intrinsically from LL. Let AA be its unique minimal normal subgroup. Conjugation identifies L/AL/A with K≤Out⁡(A)K\leq\Out(A). In type (A), we recover V=AV=A, with its natural 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-vector space structure, and Out⁡(A)=GL⁡(V)\Out(A)=\GL(V). In type (B), the simple group SS, up to isomorphism, and the integer ρ\rho are determined by A≅SρA\cong S^{\rho}.

Remark 3.4.

The word primitive in Proposition 3.3 is essential. A monolithic group whose monolith lies in the Frattini subgroup never occurs in the groups in lists (A) and (B).

3.2 The first bad crown power

Let LL be monolithic primitive. The sequence d⁡(Lt)d(L_{t}) is nondecreasing and unbounded [4, 18]. For m≥d⁡(L)m\geq d(L) an integer, define

fL​(m):=min⁡{t≥1:d⁡(Lt)>m}.f_{L}(m):=\min\{t\geq 1:d(L_{t})>m\}. (5)

Thus LfL​(m)L_{f_{L}(m)} is the first crown-based power of LL which is not mm-generated.

We record explicit descriptions of this function. Suppose first that L=V⋊KL=V\rtimes K is of abelian type. Put

D=EndK⁡(V)≅𝔽q,b=dimDV,s=dimDH1​(K,V),D=\End_{K}(V)\cong\mathbb{F}_{q},\qquad b=\dim_{D}V,\qquad s=\dim_{D}H^{1}(K,V),

and let

θ={0,if V is the trivial K-module,1,otherwise.\theta=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if $V$ is the trivial $K$-module},\\ 1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The Gaschütz–Dalla Volta–Lucchini formula gives

d⁡(Lt)=max⁡{d⁡(K),θ+⌈t+sb⌉}.d(L_{t})=\max\left\{d(K),\,\theta+\left\lceil\frac{t+s}{b}\right\rceil\right\}. (6)

Consequently, whenever d⁡(L)≤md(L)\leq m, we have that

fL​(m)=b⁡(m−θ)−s+1.f_{L}(m)=b(m-\theta)-s+1. (7)

See [4, Theorem 2.7]. Formula (6) also includes the cyclic monolith L=𝔽pL=\mathbb{F}_{p}, for which b=1b=1, s=θ=0s=\theta=0, and fL​(m)=m+1f_{L}(m)=m+1.

For a finite group GG, write

Genm⁡(G):={(g1,…,gm)∈Gm:⟨g1,…,gm⟩=G}.\Gen_{m}(G):=\{(g_{1},\ldots,g_{m})\in G^{m}:\langle g_{1},\ldots,g_{m}\rangle=G\}.

We now give an explicit formula in the nonabelian case. Let A=soc⁡(L)A=\soc(L), put K=L/AK=L/A, and write

Aut1⁡(L):={σ∈Aut⁡(L):σ⁡(ℓ)​A=ℓ​A​ for every ​ℓ∈L}.\Aut_{1}(L):=\{\sigma\in\Aut(L):\sigma(\ell)A=\ell A\text{ for every }\ell\in L\}.

For every m≥d⁡(L)m\geq d(L), Dalla Volta–Lucchini’s conditional generation formula gives the following expression. Since K=L/AK=L/A is a quotient of LL, one has d⁡(K)≤d⁡(L)≤md(K)\leq d(L)\leq m; in particular, Genm⁡(K)≠∅\Gen_{m}(K)\neq\varnothing. Thus

fL​(m)=1+|Genm⁡(L)||Aut1⁡(L)|​|Genm⁡(K)|.f_{L}(m)=1+\frac{|\Gen_{m}(L)|}{|\Aut_{1}(L)|\,|\Gen_{m}(K)|}. (8)

The quotient in (8) is an integer. It counts the Aut1⁡(L)\Aut_{1}(L)-orbits of generating lifts to LL of a fixed generating mm-tuple of KK; the number of lifts is independent of the chosen tuple, and the action is free because a generating tuple determines an automorphism. Indeed, an mm-tuple in LtL_{t} generates LtL_{t} precisely when its tt coordinate tuples generate LL and determine distinct such orbits; see [4, Theorem 2.7]. In particular, if L=SL=S is nonabelian simple, then

fS​(m)=1+|Genm⁡(S)||Aut⁡(S)|.f_{S}(m)=1+\frac{|\Gen_{m}(S)|}{|\Aut(S)|}. (9)

Thus, apart from the generation probability and the outer automorphisms, fS​(m)f_{S}(m) has size |S|m−1|S|^{m-1}.

Theorem 3.5.

Let m≥2m\geq 2, and let HH be a finite group with d⁡(H)>md(H)>m. Then there is a concrete monolithic primitive group LL, with d⁡(L)≤md(L)\leq m, such that

H↠LfL​(m).H\twoheadrightarrow L_{f_{L}(m)}.

Moreover, for every monolithic primitive group LL with d⁡(L)≤md(L)\leq m, the following bounds hold. If L=V⋊KL=V\rtimes K is of abelian type and b=dimEndK⁡(V)Vb=\dim_{\End_{K}(V)}V, then

fL​(m)>b⁡(m−2).f_{L}(m)>b(m-2). (10)

If A=soc⁡(L)A=\soc(L) is nonabelian, then

fL​(m)>|A|m−8/5>|A|m−2.f_{L}(m)>|A|^{m-8/5}>|A|^{m-2}. (11)
Proof.

Choose a quotient H0H_{0} of HH of least order subject to d⁡(H0)>md(H_{0})>m. Then

d⁡(H0/N)≤m(1≠N​⊴​H0).d(H_{0}/N)\leq m\qquad(1\neq N\trianglelefteq H_{0}).

The Dalla Volta–Lucchini reduction [4, Theorem 1.4] gives

H0≅LtH_{0}\cong L_{t}

for a monolithic primitive group LL whose monolith is either nonabelian or possessing a complement in LL, and for some t≥2t\geq 2. Proposition 3.3 puts LL in one of the two concrete forms, namely case (A)(A) or case (B)(B) of Definition 3.2. Projection onto any s<ts<t coordinates gives a quotient map Lt↠LsL_{t}\twoheadrightarrow L_{s} with non-trivial kernel. Minimality of H0H_{0} therefore gives d⁡(Ls)≤md(L_{s})\leq m for every s<ts<t. Since d⁡(Lt)>md(L_{t})>m, we have t=fL​(m)t=f_{L}(m). In particular, L=L1L=L_{1} is a proper quotient of H0H_{0}, so d⁡(L)≤md(L)\leq m.

For the bounds, let LL now be any monolithic primitive group with d⁡(L)≤md(L)\leq m. Suppose first that L=V⋊KL=V\rtimes K. If VV is the trivial KK-module, faithfulness forces K=1K=1, and (7) gives fL​(m)=m+1>b⁡(m−2)f_{L}(m)=m+1>b(m-2). If VV is a nontrivial KK-module, the Guralnick–Hoffman theorem gives

dim𝔽pH1​(K,V)≤12​dim𝔽pV[12, Theorem 1].\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}H^{1}(K,V)\leq\frac{1}{2}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}V\qquad\text{\cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{GuralnickHoffman}{}{}, Theorem 1]}}.

The field DD acts on H1​(K,V)H^{1}(K,V), so s≤b/2s\leq b/2. Since θ=1\theta=1, (7) yields

fL​(m)=b⁡(m−1)−s+1≥b⁡(m−3/2)+1>b⁡(m−2).f_{L}(m)=b(m-1)-s+1\geq b(m-3/2)+1>b(m-2).

Suppose now that AA is nonabelian, and let N≅AN\cong A be one coordinate subgroup of AfL​(m)=soc⁡(LfL​(m))A^{f_{L}(m)}=\soc(L_{f_{L}(m)}). Then

LfL​(m)/N≅LfL​(m)−1L_{f_{L}(m)}/N\cong L_{f_{L}(m)-1}

is mm-generated. If fL​(m)≤|A|m−8/5f_{L}(m)\leq|A|^{m-8/5}, then

⌈85+log|A|⁡fL​(m)⌉≤m.\left\lceil\frac{8}{5}+\log_{|A|}f_{L}(m)\right\rceil\leq m.

The Lucchini–Thakkar lifting theorem [19, Proposition 6] would then lift an mm-element generating tuple modulo NN to an mm-element generating tuple of LfL​(m)L_{f_{L}(m)}, a contradiction. This proves (11). ∎

Corollary 3.6.

Let m≥2m\geq 2, and let ℒm\mathcal{L}_{m} contain one representative from each isomorphism class of concrete monolithic primitive groups LL with d⁡(L)≤md(L)\leq m. Then

{LfL​(m):L∈ℒm}\{L_{f_{L}(m)}:L\in\mathcal{L}_{m}\}

is a set of mm-witnesses. If (Ω,ℬ,μ)(\Omega,\mathcal{B},\mu) is decent with constants M,α,δM,\alpha,\delta, then

μ⁡(Em)\displaystyle\mu(E_{m}) ≤M​∑L∈ℒm|LfL​(m)|α​|H2​(LfL​(m),ℤ)|δ|Aut⁡(LfL​(m))|\displaystyle\leq M\sum_{L\in\mathcal{L}_{m}}\frac{|L_{f_{L}(m)}|^{\alpha}|H_{2}(L_{f_{L}(m)},\mathbb{Z})|^{\delta}}{|\Aut(L_{f_{L}(m)})|} (12)
≤M​∑L∈ℒm∑n≥fL​(m)|Ln|α​|H2​(Ln,ℤ)|δ|Aut⁡(Ln)|.\displaystyle\leq M\sum_{L\in\mathcal{L}_{m}}\sum_{n\geq f_{L}(m)}\frac{|L_{n}|^{\alpha}|H_{2}(L_{n},\mathbb{Z})|^{\delta}}{|\Aut(L_{n})|}. (13)
Proof.

Combining Theorem 3.5 with Proposition 2.6 we obtain (12). Considering that the additional terms are nonnegative gives (13). ∎

4 Estimates

Throughout this section, (Ω,ℬ,μ)(\Omega,\mathcal{B},\mu) is a decent space with constants M≥1M\geq 1 and α,δ≥0\alpha,\delta\geq 0 as in (2). Put

c0=∏i=1∞(1−2−i)>0.c_{0}=\prod_{i=1}^{\infty}(1-2^{-i})>0.
Proposition 4.1.

Let LtL_{t} be a crown-based power.

  1. (i)

    Suppose that L=V⋊KL=V\rtimes K is of abelian type. Write

    D=EndK⁡(V)≅𝔽q.D=\End_{K}(V)\cong\mathbb{F}_{q}.

    Then

    |Aut⁡(Lt)|≥|GLt⁡(q)|=qt2​∏i=1t(1−q−i)≥c0​qt2.|\Aut(L_{t})|\geq|\GL_{t}(q)|=q^{t^{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}(1-q^{-i})\geq c_{0}q^{t^{2}}.
  2. (ii)

    Suppose that LL is of nonabelian type, with A=soc⁡(L)A=\soc(L). Then

    |Aut⁡(Lt)|≥|A|t⋅t!.|\Aut(L_{t})|\geq|A|^{t}\cdot t!.
Proof.

In the abelian case, Lt=Vt⋊KL_{t}=V^{t}\rtimes K. As a KK-module, VtV^{t} may be identified with V⊗DDtV\otimes_{D}D^{t}, where KK acts on the first factor. Thus every γ∈GLt⁡(D)\gamma\in\GL_{t}(D) induces the automorphism

(v,k)⟼((1⊗γ)​v,k)(v,k)\longmapsto((1\otimes\gamma)v,k)

of LtL_{t}. This gives an embedding GLt⁡(q)↪Aut⁡(Lt)\GL_{t}(q)\hookrightarrow\Aut(L_{t}). Counting ordered bases gives

|GLt⁡(q)|=qt2​∏i=1t(1−q−i),|\GL_{t}(q)|=q^{t^{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}(1-q^{-i}),

and the final inequality follows from q≥2q\geq 2.

Now suppose that AA is nonabelian. Since AA is a direct product of nonabelian simple groups, AtA^{t} is centerless. Conjugation therefore embeds AtA^{t} into Aut⁡(Lt)\Aut(L_{t}). Coordinate permutations preserve

Lt={(ℓ1,…,ℓt)∈Lt:ℓ1​A=⋯=ℓt​A}L_{t}=\{(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{t})\in L^{t}:\ell_{1}A=\cdots=\ell_{t}A\}

and give a copy of Symt\Sym_{t} in Aut⁡(Lt)\Aut(L_{t}). The two subgroups intersect trivially, and together they form

At⋊Symt≤Aut⁡(Lt).∎A^{t}\rtimes\Sym_{t}\leq\Aut(L_{t}).\qed
Lemma 4.2.

If XX is a finite dd-generated group, then

|H2​(X,ℤ)|≤|X|d.|H_{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})|\leq|X|^{d}.
Proof.

For a finite abelian group BB, write B∨=Hom⁡(B,ℚ/ℤ)B^{\vee}=\Hom(B,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}), with the contragredient action when BB is a module. We argue by induction on |X||X|. The case X=1X=1 is immediate, so assume X≠1X\neq 1 and d≥1d\geq 1. Let NN be a minimal normal subgroup of XX, and put Q=X/NQ=X/N. The Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre homology spectral sequence gives

|H2​(X,ℤ)|≤|H2​(Q,ℤ)​‖H1​(Q,H1​(N,ℤ))‖​H0​(Q,H2​(N,ℤ))|.|H_{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})|\leq|H_{2}(Q,\mathbb{Z})|\,|H_{1}(Q,H_{1}(N,\mathbb{Z}))|\,|H_{0}(Q,H_{2}(N,\mathbb{Z}))|. (14)

Since d⁡(Q)≤dd(Q)\leq d, induction gives

|H2​(Q,ℤ)|≤|Q|d.|H_{2}(Q,\mathbb{Z})|\leq|Q|^{d}.

Suppose first that NN is abelian. Then NN is an irreducible 𝔽p​[Q]\mathbb{F}_{p}[Q]-module, and H1​(Q,N)∨≅H1​(Q,N∨)H_{1}(Q,N)^{\vee}\cong H^{1}(Q,N^{\vee}). A 11-cocycle is determined by its values on a generating dd-tuple of QQ. If the action on NN is nontrivial, then (N∨)Q=0(N^{\vee})^{Q}=0, so the group of coboundaries has order |N||N|. Thus

|H1​(Q,N)|≤|N|d−1.|H_{1}(Q,N)|\leq|N|^{d-1}.

Moreover, H2(N,ℤ)=∧𝔽p2NH_{2}(N,\mathbb{Z})=\wedge^{2}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}N. The dual of its coinvariants is the space of QQ-invariant alternating forms on NN. This space embeds in HomQ⁡(N,N∨)\Hom_{Q}(N,N^{\vee}) and therefore has order at most |EndQ⁡(N)|≤|N||\End_{Q}(N)|\leq|N|. If the action on NN is trivial, then N=CpN=C_{p}, its exterior square vanishes, and the cocycle count gives |H1​(Q,N)|≤|N|d|H_{1}(Q,N)|\leq|N|^{d}. In both cases, the last two factors in (14) have product at most |N|d|N|^{d}.

Suppose now that N=SρN=S^{\rho} for a nonabelian finite simple group SS. Then H1​(N,ℤ)=0H_{1}(N,\mathbb{Z})=0, while

H2​(N,ℤ)≅H2​(S,ℤ)ρ.H_{2}(N,\mathbb{Z})\cong H_{2}(S,\mathbb{Z})^{\rho}.

The bound |H2​(S,ℤ)|≤|S||H_{2}(S,\mathbb{Z})|\leq|S| for nonabelian finite simple groups [2, pp. viii–ix, xv–xvi and 74] gives

|H0​(Q,H2​(N,ℤ))|≤|H2​(N,ℤ)|≤|N|≤|N|d.|H_{0}(Q,H_{2}(N,\mathbb{Z}))|\leq|H_{2}(N,\mathbb{Z})|\leq|N|\leq|N|^{d}.

In either case (14) gives

|H2​(X,ℤ)|≤|Q|d​|N|d=|X|d.∎|H_{2}(X,\mathbb{Z})|\leq|Q|^{d}|N|^{d}=|X|^{d}.\qed
Proposition 4.3.

Let LsL_{s} be a crown-based power.

  1. (i)

    Suppose that L=V⋊KL=V\rtimes K is of abelian type. Write

    D=EndK⁡(V)≅𝔽q,b=dimDV.D=\End_{K}(V)\cong\mathbb{F}_{q},\qquad b=\dim_{D}V.

    Then

    |H2​(Ls,ℤ)|≤|K|d⁡(K)⋅qs⁡(s+1)/2+b​s/2.|H_{2}(L_{s},\mathbb{Z})|\leq|K|^{d(K)}\cdot q^{s(s+1)/2+bs/2}. (15)

    If K=1K=1, then L=CpL=C_{p}, q=pq=p, b=1b=1, and more precisely

    |H2​(Ls,ℤ)|=p(s2).|H_{2}(L_{s},\mathbb{Z})|=p^{\binom{s}{2}}.
  2. (ii)

    Suppose that LL is of nonabelian type. Put

    A=soc⁡(L),K=L/A,N=|A|.A=\soc(L),\qquad K=L/A,\qquad N=|A|.

    Then

    |H2​(Ls,ℤ)|≤|K|d⁡(K)​Ns.|H_{2}(L_{s},\mathbb{Z})|\leq|K|^{d(K)}N^{s}. (16)
Proof.

In the abelian case, the spectral sequence for

1⟶Vs⟶Ls⟶K⟶11\longrightarrow V^{s}\longrightarrow L_{s}\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow 1

gives

|H2(Ls,ℤ)|≤|H2(K,ℤ)||H1(K,Vs)||H0(K,∧2Vs)|.|H_{2}(L_{s},\mathbb{Z})|\leq|H_{2}(K,\mathbb{Z})|\,|H_{1}(K,V^{s})|\,|H_{0}(K,\wedge^{2}V^{s})|.

By Lemma 4.2,

|H2​(K,ℤ)|≤|K|d⁡(K).|H_{2}(K,\mathbb{Z})|\leq|K|^{d(K)}.

If K≠1K\neq 1, Pontryagin duality and the Guralnick–Hoffman theorem [12, Theorem 1] applied to V∨V^{\vee} give

|H1​(K,V)|≤qb/2,|H_{1}(K,V)|\leq q^{b/2},

and hence |H1​(K,Vs)|≤qb​s/2|H_{1}(K,V^{s})|\leq q^{bs/2}.

Here tensor and exterior powers of VV are taken over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, where p=char⁡(𝔽q)p=\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{F}_{q}). Write Vs=V1⊕⋯⊕VsV^{s}=V_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{s}. Then

∧2Vs=⨁i∧2Vi⊕⨁i<jVi⊗𝔽pVj.\wedge^{2}V^{s}=\bigoplus_{i}\wedge^{2}V_{i}\oplus\bigoplus_{i<j}V_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}V_{j}.

The dual of the coinvariants of each cross-term is HomK⁡(V,V∨)\Hom_{K}(V,V^{\vee}), whose order is at most qq by Schur’s lemma. The same bound holds for a diagonal term, since invariant alternating forms form a subspace of HomK⁡(V,V∨)\Hom_{K}(V,V^{\vee}). Consequently,

|H0(K,∧2Vs)|≤qs+(s2)=qs⁡(s+1)/2.|H_{0}(K,\wedge^{2}V^{s})|\leq q^{s+\binom{s}{2}}=q^{s(s+1)/2}.

This proves (15) when K≠1K\neq 1. When K=1K=1, faithfulness and irreducibility force V=𝔽pV=\mathbb{F}_{p}, and Ls=𝔽psL_{s}=\mathbb{F}_{p}^{s}, so H2(Ls,ℤ)=∧2𝔽psH_{2}(L_{s},\mathbb{Z})=\wedge^{2}\mathbb{F}_{p}^{s}.

In the nonabelian case, AA is perfect. The spectral sequence for 1→As→Ls→K→11\to A^{s}\to L_{s}\to K\to 1 therefore gives

|H2​(Ls,ℤ)|≤|H2​(K,ℤ)|​|H0​(K,H2​(As,ℤ))|.|H_{2}(L_{s},\mathbb{Z})|\leq|H_{2}(K,\mathbb{Z})|\,|H_{0}(K,H_{2}(A^{s},\mathbb{Z}))|.

Writing A=SρA=S^{\rho} and using |H2​(S,ℤ)|≤|S||H_{2}(S,\mathbb{Z})|\leq|S|, we obtain

|H2​(As,ℤ)|=|H2​(S,ℤ)|ρ​s≤|A|s=Ns.|H_{2}(A^{s},\mathbb{Z})|=|H_{2}(S,\mathbb{Z})|^{\rho s}\leq|A|^{s}=N^{s}.

Lemma 4.2 completes the proof. ∎

The preceding automorphism and multiplier bounds give a quadratic saving in the abelian case when δ<2\delta<2. For general δ\delta, we estimate the event 𝒢↠Lt\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow L_{t} using the moment of a smaller crown LsL_{s}.

Lemma 4.4.

Suppose that L=V⋊KL=V\rtimes K is of abelian type, and put D=EndK⁡(V)≅𝔽qD=\End_{K}(V)\cong\mathbb{F}_{q}. For 1≤s≤t1\leq s\leq t,

|Sur⁡(Lt,Ls)|≥∏i=0s−1(qt−qi)≥c0​qs​t.|\Sur(L_{t},L_{s})|\geq\prod_{i=0}^{s-1}(q^{t}-q^{i})\geq c_{0}q^{st}. (17)

Consequently, in every decent probability space,

μ⁡(E⁡(Lt))≤c0−1​q−s​t​∫νLs​(𝒢)​𝑑μ.\mu(E(L_{t}))\leq c_{0}^{-1}q^{-st}\int\nu_{L_{s}}(\mathcal{G})\,d\mu. (18)
Proof.

4.1 The Liu–Wood moments

Let SS be a finite set of finite groups, and let 𝒮¯\overline{\mathcal{S}} be the smallest class containing SS and closed under subgroups, quotients, and finite direct products. For a profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, put

𝒢𝒮¯=lim←N​⊴open​𝒢𝒢/N∈𝒮¯⁡𝒢/N.\mathcal{G}^{\overline{\mathcal{S}}}=\varprojlim_{\begin{subarray}{c}N\trianglelefteq_{\mathrm{open}}\mathcal{G}\\ \mathcal{G}/N\in\overline{\mathcal{S}}\end{subarray}}\mathcal{G}/N.

The Liu–Wood space 𝒫\mathcal{P} consists of the isomorphism classes of profinite groups 𝒢\mathcal{G} for which 𝒢𝒮¯\mathcal{G}^{\overline{\mathcal{S}}} is finite for every finite SS. Its topology has basic clopen sets

US,J={𝒢∈𝒫:𝒢𝒮¯≅J},U_{S,J}=\{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{P}:\mathcal{G}^{\overline{\mathcal{S}}}\cong J\},

where JJ ranges over the finite groups in 𝒮¯\overline{\mathcal{S}}, up to isomorphism.

Proposition 4.8.

For every finite group HH and every u∈ℤu\in\mathbb{Z}, the function νH\nu_{H} is measurable on 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and

∫𝒫νH​(𝒢)​d​μu​(𝒢)=|H|−u.\int_{\mathcal{P}}\nu_{H}(\mathcal{G})\,d\mu_{u}(\mathcal{G})=|H|^{-u}.
Proof.

Take S={H}S=\{H\}. Every homomorphism 𝒢→H\mathcal{G}\to H factors uniquely through 𝒢𝒮¯\mathcal{G}^{\overline{\mathcal{S}}}, so

Sur⁡(𝒢,H)=Sur⁡(𝒢𝒮¯,H).\Sur(\mathcal{G},H)=\Sur(\mathcal{G}^{\overline{\mathcal{S}}},H).

It follows that 𝒢↦|Sur⁡(𝒢,H)|\mathcal{G}\mapsto|\Sur(\mathcal{G},H)| is constant on each basic clopen set US,JU_{S,J}, and hence is continuous and measurable.

The finite model satisfies

𝔼​|Sur⁡(Xu,n,H)|=|Sur⁡(F^n,H)||H|n+u,\mathbb{E}\,|\Sur(X_{u,n},H)|=\frac{|\Sur(\widehat{F}_{n},H)|}{|H|^{n+u}}, (28)

since an epimorphism F^n↠H\widehat{F}_{n}\twoheadrightarrow H factors through Xu,nX_{u,n} precisely when the n+un+u independent Haar-random relators land in its kernel, an event of probability |H|−(n+u)|H|^{-(n+u)}. Since a fixed finite group is generated by a random nn-tuple with probability tending to 11,

limn→∞𝔼​|Sur⁡(Xu,n,H)|=|H|−u.\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}|\Sur(X_{u,n},H)|=|H|^{-u}. (29)

We verify uniform integrability. For a pair of epimorphisms φ,ψ:F^n↠H\varphi,\psi:\widehat{F}_{n}\twoheadrightarrow H, the image of (φ,ψ)(\varphi,\psi) is a subdirect subgroup of H×HH\times H. Pairs with image JJ are in bijection with Sur⁡(F^n,J)\Sur(\widehat{F}_{n},J). Thus

𝔼​|Sur⁡(Xu,n,H)|2=∑J≤H×HJ​ subdirect|Sur⁡(F^n,J)||J|n+u≤∑J≤H×HJ​ subdirect|J|−u.\mathbb{E}|\Sur(X_{u,n},H)|^{2}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}J\leq H\times H\\ J\text{ subdirect}\end{subarray}}\frac{|\Sur(\widehat{F}_{n},J)|}{|J|^{n+u}}\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}J\leq H\times H\\ J\text{ subdirect}\end{subarray}}|J|^{-u}.

The last sum is finite and independent of nn. Thus the random variables |Sur⁡(Xu,n,H)||\Sur(X_{u,n},H)| are uniformly bounded in L2L^{2}, hence uniformly integrable.

The laws of Xu,nX_{u,n} converge weakly to μu\mu_{u} [22, Theorem 1.1]. Since the epimorphism-counting function is continuous, its values converge in distribution. Uniform integrability and (29) now imply the asserted identity. ∎

Corollary 4.9.

For every u∈ℤu\in\mathbb{Z}, the Liu–Wood random profinite group is topologically finitely generated with probability 11.

Proof.

Apply Theorem 1.1 with M=1M=1, α=max⁡{0,−u}\alpha=\max\{0,-u\} and δ=0\delta=0, using Proposition 4.8. ∎

4.2 The Sawin–Wood moments

Let Mg,LM_{g,L} be the random closed oriented 33-manifold obtained from a genus-gg Heegaard splitting whose gluing map is a uniform random word of length LL in a fixed finite generating set of the mapping class group containing the identity. Sawin and Wood prove that, first letting L→∞L\to\infty and then g→∞g\to\infty, the laws of π1^​(Mg,L)\widehat{\pi_{1}}(M_{g,L}) converge to a probability measure μSW\mu_{\mathrm{SW}} on their space Prof\operatorname{Prof} of profinite groups having only finitely many open subgroups of each index [30, Theorem 1.2]. This is the space 𝒫\mathcal{P} above, with the same topology [30, Section 1.3 and Lemma 8.8]. For every finite group HH, their moment calculation gives

∫𝒫νH​(𝒢)​d​μSW​(𝒢)=|H|​|H2​(H,ℤ)||H1​(H,ℤ)|.\int_{\mathcal{P}}\nu_{H}(\mathcal{G})\,d\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}(\mathcal{G})=\frac{|H|\,|H_{2}(H,\mathbb{Z})|}{|H_{1}(H,\mathbb{Z})|}. (30)

The limiting moment is computed by Dunfield and Thurston [7, Theorem 6.21]; Sawin and Wood’s moment-convergence argument [30, Proposition 4.6 and Section 9.3] shows that it is the moment of the limiting measure, rather than merely the limit of the finite-stage moments.

Since |H1​(H,ℤ)|≥1|H_{1}(H,\mathbb{Z})|\geq 1, equation (30) implies

∫𝒫νH​(𝒢)​d​μSW​(𝒢)≤|H|⋅|H2​(H,ℤ)|.\int_{\mathcal{P}}\nu_{H}(\mathcal{G})\,d\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}(\mathcal{G})\leq|H|\cdot|H_{2}(H,\mathbb{Z})|.

Thus (𝒫,ℬ,μSW)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{B},\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}) is decent with constants M=1M=1 and α=δ=1\alpha=\delta=1.

Corollary 4.10.

A μSW\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}-random profinite group is topologically finitely generated with probability 11.

Proof.

Apply Theorem 1.1 to the decent space (𝒫,ℬ,μSW)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{B},\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}). ∎

This answers the question posed by Sawin and Wood [30, Section 10.3].

5 Finite presentation

We first show that a uniform bound on the number of normal generators in finite quotients gives the same bound in the profinite group.

In the presentation displays in the introduction, ⟨x1,…,xr⟩¯\overline{\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\rangle} denotes the closed normal closure of the relators in the ambient free profinite group; the same convention applies to the defining display for Xu,nX_{u,n}.

Lemma 5.1.

Let FF be a profinite group, let R​⊴​FR\trianglelefteq F be closed, and let r≥0r\geq 0 be an integer. Suppose that R​U/URU/U is normally generated by at most rr elements in F/UF/U for every open normal subgroup U​⊴​FU\trianglelefteq F. Then RR is the closed normal closure in FF of at most rr elements.

Proof.

For every open normal subgroup U​⊴​FU\trianglelefteq F, let

CU={(x1,…,xr)∈Rr:x1U,…,xrU normally generate RU/U in F/U}.C_{U}=\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r})\in R^{r}:x_{1}U,\ldots,x_{r}U\text{ normally generate }RU/U\text{ in }F/U\}.

For r=0r=0, we interpret R0R^{0} as a one-point space. Each CUC_{U} is nonempty: lift normal generators of R​U/URU/U to RR and add identities if necessary. It is clopen, since membership depends only on the image in (F/U)r(F/U)^{r}.

The family {CU}\{C_{U}\} has the finite-intersection property. Indeed, if U0=U1∩⋯∩UsU_{0}=U_{1}\cap\cdots\cap U_{s}, then

CU0⊆CU1∩⋯∩CUs.C_{U_{0}}\subseteq C_{U_{1}}\cap\cdots\cap C_{U_{s}}.

Compactness of RrR^{r} therefore gives a tuple

(x1,…,xr)∈⋂UCU.(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r})\in\bigcap_{U}C_{U}.

Let

R0=⟨x1,…,xr⟩F¯.R_{0}=\overline{\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\rangle^{F}}.

Then R0​U=R​UR_{0}U=RU for every open normal UU. Since R0R_{0} and RR are closed,

R0=⋂UR0​U=⋂UR​U=R.R_{0}=\bigcap_{U}R_{0}U=\bigcap_{U}RU=R.

∎

5.1 The Sawin–Wood model

For integers d,r≥0d,r\geq 0, let

FPd,r={𝒢∈𝒫:𝒢≅F^d/⟨x1,…,xr⟩F^d¯ for some x1,…,xr∈F^d}.\operatorname{FP}_{d,r}=\Bigl\{\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{P}:\mathcal{G}\cong\widehat{F}_{d}/\overline{\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\rangle^{\widehat{F}_{d}}}\text{ for some }x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\in\widehat{F}_{d}\Bigr\}.

Presentations with fewer than rr relators are included by using identity relators.

Proposition 5.2.

For all integers d,r≥0d,r\geq 0, the set FPd,r\operatorname{FP}_{d,r} is closed in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The set of finitely presented groups is Borel. The set of finitely generated groups admitting a presentation with d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) generators and d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) relators is also Borel. It remains Borel if we require that every profinite presentation have at least d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) relators.

Proof.

Consider the quotient map

qd,r:F^dr⟶𝒫,(x1,…,xr)⟼F^d/⟨x1,…,xr⟩F^d¯.q_{d,r}:\widehat{F}_{d}^{r}\longrightarrow\mathcal{P},\qquad(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r})\longmapsto\widehat{F}_{d}/\overline{\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\rangle^{\widehat{F}_{d}}}.

Its image is FPd,r\operatorname{FP}_{d,r}. The map is continuous. Indeed, if SS is a finite set of finite groups, put PS=(F^d)𝒮¯P_{S}=(\widehat{F}_{d})^{\overline{\mathcal{S}}} and let x¯i\bar{x}_{i} denote the image of xix_{i} in PSP_{S}. The universal property of level completion gives

qd,r​(x1,…,xr)𝒮¯≅PS/⟨x¯1,…,x¯r⟩PS.q_{d,r}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r})^{\overline{\mathcal{S}}}\cong P_{S}/\langle\bar{x}_{1},\ldots,\bar{x}_{r}\rangle^{P_{S}}.

Its isomorphism class therefore depends only on the images of the xix_{i} in the finite group PSP_{S}. Thus the inverse image under qd,rq_{d,r} of every basic clopen subset of 𝒫\mathcal{P} is clopen.

The space 𝒫\mathcal{P} is Hausdorff [30, Section 1]. Thus FPd,r\operatorname{FP}_{d,r} is closed, being the image of a compact space under a continuous map. Taking a countable union over d,rd,r proves the first Borel assertion. The sets {𝒢:d⁡(𝒢)=d}\{\mathcal{G}:d(\mathcal{G})=d\} are Borel by Section 2. The set of finitely generated groups admitting the stated presentation is

⋃d≥0({𝒢:d⁡(𝒢)=d}∩FPd,d),\bigcup_{d\geq 0}\bigl(\{\mathcal{G}:d(\mathcal{G})=d\}\cap\operatorname{FP}_{d,d}\bigr),

and is Borel as well. The additional requirement excludes precisely the Borel set

⋃n,r≥0({𝒢:d⁡(𝒢)>r}∩FPn,r),\bigcup_{n,r\geq 0}\bigl(\{\mathcal{G}:d(\mathcal{G})>r\}\cap\operatorname{FP}_{n,r}\bigr),

consisting of groups admitting a presentation with fewer than d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) relators. This proves the final assertion. The condition that every finite profinite presentation have at least as many relators as generators is Borel as well: it excludes precisely

⋃n>r≥0FPn,r.\bigcup_{n>r\geq 0}\operatorname{FP}_{n,r}.

∎

Lemma 5.3.

Let PP be a finite group, let A​⊴​PA\trianglelefteq P, and let r≥1r\geq 1. For every prime pp, put

Ap=A/[A,A]​Ap,A_{p}=A/[A,A]A^{p},

viewed as an 𝔽p​[P/A]\mathbb{F}_{p}[P/A]-module. If every ApA_{p} is generated by at most rr elements as a module, then AA is normally generated in PP by at most rr elements.

Proof.

The assertion is immediate if A=1A=1. Let Φ\Phi be the intersection of the maximal proper subgroups of AA that are normal in PP. A tuple normally generates AA in PP if and only if its image normally generates A/ΦA/\Phi.

Choose M1,…,MkM_{1},\ldots,M_{k} with intersection Φ\Phi such that none can be omitted. For each ii, the image of ⋂j<iMj\bigcap_{j<i}M_{j} in A/MiA/M_{i} is nontrivial and normal under PP. It is therefore all of A/MiA/M_{i}. Here the empty intersection means AA. Induction gives a PP-equivariant isomorphism

A/Φ≅∏i=1kA/Mi.A/\Phi\cong\prod_{i=1}^{k}A/M_{i}.

Each factor is either elementary abelian or a direct product of nonabelian simple groups. Write this product as B×CB\times C, where BB is the product of the abelian factors and CC is the product of the nonabelian factors. For every prime pp, the Sylow pp-subgroup BpB_{p} of BB is an 𝔽p​[P/A]\mathbb{F}_{p}[P/A]-module quotient of ApA_{p}, so it is generated by at most rr elements. Combining these tuples over all pp gives rr elements that normally generate BB under PP.

Extend this tuple to B×CB\times C so that the first element has a nonidentity component in every simple direct factor of CC. Commutators with each factor show that the normal closure of this element meets that factor nontrivially. It therefore contains the factor. Thus the tuple normally generates B×CB\times C under PP. Lifting it to AA proves the assertion. ∎

The next proposition follows from Lubotzky’s presentation formula [20, Theorems 3.1 and 5.1]. We include a proof. Throughout this section, cohomology and homomorphisms of profinite modules are continuous.

Proposition 5.4.

dimDH2​(𝒢,V)≤dimDH1​(𝒢,V).\dim_{D}H^{2}(\mathcal{G},V)\leq\dim_{D}H^{1}(\mathcal{G},V). (31)

Then 𝒢\mathcal{G} has a profinite presentation with dd generators and at most dd relations.

Rp=R/[R,R]​Rp¯.R_{p}=R/\overline{[R,R]R^{p}}.

If ξV=0\xi_{V}=0 for the trivial module and ξV=1\xi_{V}=1 otherwise, then

dimDH1​(F,V)=(d−ξV)​dimDV.\dim_{D}H^{1}(F,V)=(d-\xi_{V})\dim_{D}V.

dimDHom𝒢⁡(Rp,V)≤(d−ξV)​dimD(V)≤d⋅dimD(V).\dim_{D}\Hom_{\mathcal{G}}(R_{p},V)\leq(d-\xi_{V})\dim_{D}(V)\leq d\cdot\dim_{D}(V). (33)

For every prime pp, the 𝔽p​[QU]\mathbb{F}_{p}[Q_{U}]-module

is a quotient of RpR_{p}. If VV is a simple 𝔽p​[QU]\mathbb{F}_{p}[Q_{U}]-module, inflate it to a 𝒢\mathcal{G}-module. Composition with Rp↠AU,pR_{p}\twoheadrightarrow A_{U,p} gives

dimDHomQU⁡(AU,p,V)≤dimDHom𝒢⁡(Rp,V)≤d⋅dimD(V).\dim_{D}\Hom_{Q_{U}}(A_{U,p},V)\leq\dim_{D}\Hom_{\mathcal{G}}(R_{p},V)\leq d\cdot\dim_{D}(V).

The multiplicity of VV in N/J​NN/JN is dimEndQ⁡(V)HomQ⁡(N,V)\dim_{\End_{Q}(V)}\Hom_{Q}(N,V), while its multiplicity in 𝔽p​[Q]/J\mathbb{F}_{p}[Q]/J is dimEndQ⁡(V)V\dim_{\End_{Q}(V)}V. Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Sawin and Wood prove that the support of μSW\mu_{\mathrm{SW}} is the closure in 𝒫\mathcal{P} of the profinite completions of fundamental groups of closed oriented 33-manifolds [30, Theorems 1.2 and 1.5]. For every 𝒢\mathcal{G} in this support, there is a homomorphism

τ:H3​(𝒢,ℚ/ℤ)⟶ℚ/ℤ\tau:H^{3}(\mathcal{G},\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\longrightarrow\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}

with the following properties. For every prime pp and every finite simple 𝔽p​[[𝒢]]\mathbb{F}_{p}[[\mathcal{G}]]-module VV, put V∨=Hom𝔽p⁡(V,𝔽p)V^{\vee}=\Hom_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(V,\mathbb{F}_{p}). Then

dim𝔽pH1​(𝒢,V)=dim𝔽pH1​(𝒢,V∨),\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}H^{1}(\mathcal{G},V)=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}H^{1}(\mathcal{G},V^{\vee}), (34)
H2​(𝒢,V)×H1​(𝒢,V∨)⟶ℚ/ℤ,(α,β)⟼τ⁡(α⌣β),\displaystyle H^{2}(\mathcal{G},V)\times H^{1}(\mathcal{G},V^{\vee})\longrightarrow\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z},\qquad(\alpha,\beta)\longmapsto\tau(\alpha\smile\beta), (35)

where the pairing is nondegenerate in its first variable. Here the cup product uses evaluation V⊗𝔽pV∨→𝔽pV\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}V^{\vee}\to\mathbb{F}_{p} followed by the homomorphism 𝔽p→ℚ/ℤ\mathbb{F}_{p}\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z} sending 11 to 1/p1/p.

Suppose now that d⁡(𝒢)<∞d(\mathcal{G})<\infty. The group H1​(𝒢,V∨)H^{1}(\mathcal{G},V^{\vee}) is finite, since a continuous 11-cocycle is determined by its values on a finite generating tuple. The pairing (35) gives an injection

H2​(𝒢,V)↪Hom⁡(H1​(𝒢,V∨),ℚ/ℤ).H^{2}(\mathcal{G},V)\hookrightarrow\Hom\bigl(H^{1}(\mathcal{G},V^{\vee}),\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\bigr).

Thus H2​(𝒢,V)H^{2}(\mathcal{G},V) is finite and, by (34),

dim𝔽pH2​(𝒢,V)≤dim𝔽pH1​(𝒢,V).\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}H^{2}(\mathcal{G},V)\leq\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}H^{1}(\mathcal{G},V).

Dividing by [D:𝔽p][D:\mathbb{F}_{p}], where D=End𝒢⁡(V)D=\End_{\mathcal{G}}(V), gives (31). Proposition 5.4 therefore gives a presentation with d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) generators and at most d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) relators.

By Corollary 4.10, the hypothesis d⁡(𝒢)<∞d(\mathcal{G})<\infty holds for μSW\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}-almost every 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The support has full measure: 𝒫\mathcal{P} has a countable clopen basis, so the complement of the support is a countable union of null basic opens. Thus this presentation exists almost surely.

To prove that the number of relators is minimal, fix a prime pp. For k≥1k\geq 1, let CpkC_{p^{k}} be the cyclic group of order pkp^{k}. Its Schur multiplier is trivial, so (30) gives

𝔼μSW​νℤ/pk​ℤ=1.\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}}\nu_{\mathbb{Z}/p^{k}\mathbb{Z}}=1.

The free action of Aut⁡(ℤ/pk​ℤ)\Aut(\mathbb{Z}/p^{k}\mathbb{Z}) on epimorphisms, as in Remark 2.2, therefore gives

μSW​{𝒢:𝒢↠ℤ/pk​ℤ}≤1pk−1​(p−1).\mu_{\mathrm{SW}}\{\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/p^{k}\mathbb{Z}\}\leq\frac{1}{p^{k-1}(p-1)}.

These events are measurable and decreasing in kk, so their intersection has measure zero. The maximal abelian pro-pp quotient ApA_{p} of a finitely generated profinite group is a finitely generated ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module. If ApA_{p} were infinite, it would have a quotient isomorphic to ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}, and hence quotients CpkC_{p^{k}} for every kk. Thus ApA_{p} is finite almost surely.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a finitely generated group with this property. A presentation with infinitely many generators and finitely many relators has an infinite elementary abelian pp-quotient. It therefore cannot present 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Consider a presentation of 𝒢\mathcal{G} with nn generators and rr relators y1,…,yr∈F^ny_{1},\ldots,y_{r}\in\widehat{F}_{n}. Passing to the maximal abelian pro-pp quotient gives

Ap≅ℤpn/∑i=1rℤp​y¯i,A_{p}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{n}/\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb{Z}_{p}\bar{y}_{i},

where y¯i\bar{y}_{i} is the image of yiy_{i} in ℤpn\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{n}. Since ApA_{p} is finite, these vectors span ℚpn\mathbb{Q}_{p}^{n}. Hence r≥n≥d⁡(𝒢)r\geq n\geq d(\mathcal{G}). Every profinite presentation of 𝒢\mathcal{G} therefore has at least d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) relators. The presentation already constructed attains this bound with d⁡(𝒢)d(\mathcal{G}) generators. Proposition 5.2 gives the asserted measurability. ∎

5.2 The Liu–Wood model

We now specialize to the probability space 𝒫\mathcal{P} of small profinite groups. Retain the notation 𝒮¯\overline{\mathcal{S}} from the end of Section 4, and write

Fd,S:=(F^d)𝒮¯.F_{d,S}:=(\widehat{F}_{d})^{\overline{\mathcal{S}}}.

For finite SS, this is the finite free pro-𝒮¯\overline{\mathcal{S}} group on dd generators.

We give an alternative, cohomological proof of Liu and Wood’s [22, Lemma 13.1].

with E∈𝒮¯E\in\overline{\mathcal{S}}. The diagonal copy Δ​V\Delta V is normal in E×HEE\times_{H}E, and

(E×HE)/Δ​V≅V⋊H.(E\times_{H}E)/\Delta V\cong V\rtimes H.

Indeed, the diagonal copy of EE gives a section after quotienting by Δ​V\Delta V. Thus V⋊H∈𝒮¯V\rtimes H\in\overline{\mathcal{S}}.

By the universal property of PjP_{j}, the lifts of its distinguished generators to V⋊HV\rtimes H can be chosen arbitrarily. Hence a 11-cocycle Pj→VP_{j}\to V is specified by any jj values in VV. If ξV=0\xi_{V}=0 for the trivial module and ξV=1\xi_{V}=1 otherwise, then

dimDH1​(Pj,V)=(j−ξV)​v.\dim_{D}H^{1}(P_{j},V)=(j-\xi_{V})v.

Put

Kj=ker⁡(H2​(H,V)⟶H2​(Pj,V)).K_{j}=\ker\bigl(H^{2}(H,V)\longrightarrow H^{2}(P_{j},V)\bigr).

It follows that

md​(V)=mn​(V)−(n−d)​v≤r​v.m_{d}(V)=m_{n}(V)-(n-d)v\leq rv.

This also holds when md​(V)=0m_{d}(V)=0. The module criterion in the proof of Proposition 5.4 shows that every Ad/[Ad,Ad]​AdpA_{d}/[A_{d},A_{d}]A_{d}^{p} is generated by at most rr elements. Lemma 5.3 now gives the assertion. ∎

Put

FP:=⋃d,r≥0FPd,r.\operatorname{FP}:=\bigcup_{d,r\geq 0}\operatorname{FP}_{d,r}.
Proposition 5.6.

The Borel σ\sigma-algebra of 𝒫\mathcal{P} is generated by the functions νA\nu_{A}, where AA ranges over the finite groups. In particular, FPd,r\operatorname{FP}_{d,r} and FP\operatorname{FP} belong to this σ\sigma-algebra.

Each νA\nu_{A} is continuous: its value is determined by the finite completion 𝒢{A}¯\mathcal{G}^{\overline{\{A\}}}. Conversely, for a finite set SS and a finite pro-𝒮¯\overline{\mathcal{S}} group HH,

For a nonabelian finite simple group SS and 𝒢∈𝒫\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{P}, put

Lemma 5.7.

Let S1,…,SeS_{1},\ldots,S_{e} be pairwise nonisomorphic nonabelian finite simple groups and let t1,…,te≥0t_{1},\ldots,t_{e}\geq 0. For every 𝒢∈𝒫\mathcal{G}\in\mathcal{P},

Proof of Theorem 1.3.
