7 Universal perfect profinite groups

Nikolov asked whether, for each d>1d>1, there is a finitely generated perfect profinite group whose finite quotients include every finite perfect dd-generated group [25, Conjecture B1]. We prove the following stronger statement. Here and below, “dd-generated” means “generated by at most dd elements.”

Theorem 7.1.

Let d≥2d\geq 2.

  1. (i)

    Every finite family H1,…,HsH_{1},\ldots,H_{s} of finite dd-generated perfect groups has a finite dd-generated perfect common cover: there is a finite perfect group CC, with d⁡(C)≤dd(C)\leq d, and epimorphisms

    C↠Hi(1≤i≤s).C\twoheadrightarrow H_{i}\qquad(1\leq i\leq s).
  2. (ii)

    There is a topologically dd-generated profinite group UdU_{d} such that

    Ud=[Ud,Ud]U_{d}=[U_{d},U_{d}]

    as an abstract group and whose finite continuous quotients are precisely the finite perfect groups HH with d⁡(H)≤dd(H)\leq d.

  3. (iii)

    UdU_{d} is unique: if 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a topologically dd-generated profinite group with 𝒱=[𝒱,𝒱]¯\mathcal{V}=\overline{[\mathcal{V},\mathcal{V}]} whose finite continuous quotients include every finite perfect dd-generated group, then 𝒱≅Ud\mathcal{V}\cong U_{d} as topological groups.

  4. (iv)

    UdU_{d} is projective, d⁡(Ud)=dd(U_{d})=d, and UdU_{d} admits a profinite presentation with dd generators and dd relators. Every profinite presentation of UdU_{d} has at least dd relators.

To construct UdU_{d}, we show that any two finite perfect dd-generated groups have a finite perfect dd-generated common cover. We construct the common cover by induction along a chief series of one of the two groups, applying Lemma 7.3 at each step. Its proof uses Frattini subgroups in the central case and Gaschütz’s lifting lemma in the noncentral case.

We first record the Frattini observation used in the central case.

Lemma 7.2.

Let PP be a finite perfect group. Then every central subgroup Z≤Z⁡(P)Z\leq Z(P) is contained in Frat⁡(P)\Frat(P). Consequently, if P↠QP\twoheadrightarrow Q has central kernel, then

d⁡(P)=d⁡(Q).d(P)=d(Q).
Proof.

Suppose that a maximal subgroup M<PM<P does not contain ZZ. Then P=M​ZP=MZ. Since ZZ is central, MM is normal in PP, so P/MP/M is a nontrivial abelian quotient of PP, contrary to P=[P,P]P=[P,P]. Thus every maximal subgroup contains ZZ, and hence Z≤Frat⁡(P)Z\leq\Frat(P).

For the last assertion, a subset of PP generates PP if and only if its image generates P/ZP/Z whenever Z≤Frat⁡(P)Z\leq\Frat(P). Applying this to the central kernel of P↠QP\twoheadrightarrow Q gives d⁡(P)=d⁡(Q)d(P)=d(Q). ∎

Lemma 7.3.

Let d≥1d\geq 1 be an integer, let AA, BB, and QQ be finite perfect groups, and let

α:A↠Q,β:B↠Q\alpha:A\twoheadrightarrow Q,\qquad\beta:B\twoheadrightarrow Q

be epimorphisms. Suppose that N=ker⁡βN=\ker\beta is a minimal normal subgroup of BB. If d⁡(A),d⁡(B)≤dd(A),d(B)\leq d, then there is a finite perfect group CC with d⁡(C)≤dd(C)\leq d and epimorphisms πA:C↠A\pi_{A}:C\twoheadrightarrow A and πB:C↠B\pi_{B}:C\twoheadrightarrow B such that α∘πA=β∘πB\alpha\circ\pi_{A}=\beta\circ\pi_{B}.

Proof.

Form the fibre product

E=A×QB={(a,b)∈A×B:α⁡(a)=β⁡(b)}.E=A\times_{Q}B=\{(a,b)\in A\times B:\alpha(a)=\beta(b)\}.

We distinguish the central and noncentral cases.

Suppose first that N≤Z⁡(B)N\leq Z(B). We identify NN with 1×N≤E1\times N\leq E; it is central in EE, and E/N≅AE/N\cong A. Since AA is perfect, the image of E′E^{\prime} in E/NE/N is all of E/NE/N, so

E=E′​N.E=E^{\prime}N.

The centrality of NN now gives

E′=[E,E]=[E′​N,E′​N]=[E′,E′]=E′′.E^{\prime}=[E,E]=[E^{\prime}N,E^{\prime}N]=[E^{\prime},E^{\prime}]=E^{\prime\prime}.

Thus C:=E′C:=E^{\prime} is perfect. Both coordinate projections of EE are surjective, and the image of a derived group under an epimorphism is the derived group of the image. Since AA and BB are perfect, the restrictions

E′↠A,E′↠BE^{\prime}\twoheadrightarrow A,\qquad E^{\prime}\twoheadrightarrow B

are therefore surjective. The kernel of E′↠AE^{\prime}\twoheadrightarrow A is contained in the central group NN. Lemma 7.2 then yields

d⁡(E′)=d⁡(A)≤d.d(E^{\prime})=d(A)\leq d.

Suppose now that N≰Z⁡(B)N\not\leq Z(B). Choose a generating dd-tuple (q1,…,qd)(q_{1},\ldots,q_{d}) of QQ, padding with identity elements if necessary. Gaschütz’s lifting lemma [10] gives generating tuples (a1,…,ad)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{d}) of AA and (b1,…,bd)(b_{1},\ldots,b_{d}) of BB such that

α⁡(ai)=qi=β⁡(bi)(1≤i≤d).\alpha(a_{i})=q_{i}=\beta(b_{i})\qquad(1\leq i\leq d).

Put

D=⟨(a1,b1),…,(ad,bd)⟩≤E.D=\langle(a_{1},b_{1}),\ldots,(a_{d},b_{d})\rangle\leq E.

Both coordinate projections of DD are surjective. Set

K=D∩(1×N).K=D\cap(1\times N).

Under the identification 1×N≅N1\times N\cong N, the group KK is normal in BB: it is normal in DD, and the second projection D↠BD\twoheadrightarrow B is surjective. The minimal normality of NN therefore gives K=1K=1 or K=NK=N.

If K=1K=1, then D↠AD\twoheadrightarrow A is an isomorphism. Hence DD is a perfect dd-generated common cover of AA and BB. If K=NK=N, then D=ED=E. Since NN is minimal normal and noncentral in BB, one has

[N,B]=N.[N,B]=N.

The action of EE on NN is the action induced by its projection onto BB, so [N,E]=N[N,E]=N. Moreover E/N≅AE/N\cong A is perfect. It follows that E=E′​NE=E^{\prime}N and N≤E′N\leq E^{\prime}, whence E=E′E=E^{\prime}. Thus in this case D=ED=E is again a perfect dd-generated common cover. ∎

The same argument applies to finitely many central extensions of a fixed perfect group.

Corollary 7.4.

Let QQ be a finite perfect group and let

βi:Bi↠Q(1≤i≤s)\beta_{i}:B_{i}\twoheadrightarrow Q\qquad(1\leq i\leq s)

be finite perfect central extensions. Form their fibre product over QQ,

E=B1×Q⋯×QBs.E=B_{1}\times_{Q}\cdots\times_{Q}B_{s}.

Then E′E^{\prime} is a finite perfect common cover of the BiB_{i}, and

d⁡(E′)=d⁡(Q).d(E^{\prime})=d(Q).
Proof.

The kernel ZZ of E↠QE\twoheadrightarrow Q is central. Since QQ is perfect, E=E′​ZE=E^{\prime}Z, and therefore

E′=[E′​Z,E′​Z]=[E′,E′].E^{\prime}=[E^{\prime}Z,E^{\prime}Z]=[E^{\prime},E^{\prime}].

Each projection E↠BiE\twoheadrightarrow B_{i} is surjective, so it maps E′E^{\prime} onto Bi′=BiB_{i}^{\prime}=B_{i}. Finally, the kernel of E′↠QE^{\prime}\twoheadrightarrow Q is central in the perfect group E′E^{\prime}. Lemma 7.2 gives d⁡(E′)=d⁡(Q)d(E^{\prime})=d(Q). ∎

Remark 7.5.

For a monolithic primitive group LL and a profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, put

κL​(𝒢)=sup{t≥1:𝒢↠Lt},sup∅=0.\kappa_{L}(\mathcal{G})=\sup\{t\geq 1:\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow L_{t}\},\qquad\sup\varnothing=0.

By Proposition 6.1, a finite group GG satisfies d⁡(G)≤dd(G)\leq d if and only if κL​(G)<fL​(d)\kappa_{L}(G)<f_{L}(d) for every LL, when d≥2d\geq 2.

In the central case of Lemma 7.3, the groups C=E′C=E^{\prime} and AA have the same primitive crown quotients. Indeed, Frat⁡(L)=1\Frat(L)=1 for every monolithic primitive group LL. The coordinate maps Lt↠LL_{t}\twoheadrightarrow L have trivial common kernel, so Frat⁡(Lt)=1\Frat(L_{t})=1 as well. Since ker⁡(C↠A)≤Frat⁡(C)\ker(C\twoheadrightarrow A)\leq\Frat(C), every epimorphism C↠LtC\twoheadrightarrow L_{t} factors through AA. Thus

κL​(C)=κL​(A)\kappa_{L}(C)=\kappa_{L}(A)

for every LL.

In the noncentral case, the subgroup DD generated by the lifted dd-tuple either maps isomorphically onto AA or equals A×QBA\times_{Q}B. Both cases give a perfect common cover with at most dd generators. The crown criterion therefore bounds all its crown multiplicities by fL​(d)−1f_{L}(d)-1. Proposition 7.7 describes the multiplicities in the limit: each perfect monolithic primitive group LL has crown multiplicity fL​(d)−1f_{L}(d)-1.

Proposition 7.6.

Let d≥1d\geq 1 be an integer. Any two finite perfect dd-generated groups have a finite perfect dd-generated common cover.

Proof.

Let AA and BB be finite perfect groups with d⁡(A),d⁡(B)≤dd(A),d(B)\leq d. Choose a chief series

1=N0<N1<⋯<Nr=B.1=N_{0}<N_{1}<\cdots<N_{r}=B.

Thus Nj+1/NjN_{j+1}/N_{j} is a minimal normal subgroup of B/NjB/N_{j} for 0≤j<r0\leq j<r. Every quotient B/NjB/N_{j} is perfect.

We descend from B/Nr=1B/N_{r}=1 to B/N0=BB/N_{0}=B. Start with Cr=AC_{r}=A, equipped with the unique epimorphism Cr↠B/NrC_{r}\twoheadrightarrow B/N_{r}. Suppose that a finite perfect dd-generated group Cj+1C_{j+1} has been constructed which maps onto AA and onto B/Nj+1B/N_{j+1}. Apply Lemma 7.3 to

Cj+1↠B/Nj+1andB/Nj↠B/Nj+1.C_{j+1}\twoheadrightarrow B/N_{j+1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad B/N_{j}\twoheadrightarrow B/N_{j+1}.

It gives a finite perfect dd-generated group CjC_{j} mapping onto both Cj+1C_{j+1} and B/NjB/N_{j}. At the end, C0C_{0} maps onto both AA and BB. This proves the assertion for two groups; induction gives the assertion for any finite family. ∎

7.1 Existence of the universal group

Proof of Theorem 7.1(i) and (ii).

Part (i) is Proposition 7.6.

For part (ii), enumerate the isomorphism classes of finite perfect dd-generated groups as

H1,H2,….H_{1},H_{2},\ldots.

Start with P1=H1P_{1}=H_{1}. Using Proposition 7.6 recursively, construct finite perfect dd-generated groups PnP_{n} and epimorphisms

Pn+1↠Pn,Pn↠Hn.P_{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow P_{n},\qquad P_{n}\twoheadrightarrow H_{n}.

By composition, PnP_{n} maps onto every HiH_{i} with i≤ni\leq n. Put

Ud=lim←n⁡Pn.U_{d}=\varprojlim_{n}P_{n}.

The projection Ud↠PnU_{d}\twoheadrightarrow P_{n} is surjective, so every HnH_{n} is a continuous quotient of UdU_{d}.

Every finite continuous quotient of UdU_{d} factors through some PnP_{n}, since the kernels of the projections form a basis of open neighbourhoods of the identity. It is therefore perfect and dd-generated. Proposition 2.3 gives d⁡(Ud)≤dd(U_{d})\leq d. Thus the finite continuous quotients of UdU_{d} are precisely the finite perfect dd-generated groups.

Finally, since every finite continuous quotient of UdU_{d} is perfect, the abstract derived subgroup [Ud,Ud][U_{d},U_{d}] is dense in UdU_{d}. The derived subgroup of a topologically finitely generated profinite group is closed by the uniform commutator theorem of Nikolov and Segal [26, Theorem 1.4]. Therefore

Ud=[Ud,Ud],U_{d}=[U_{d},U_{d}],

as required. ∎

Proposition 7.7.

Let d≥2d\geq 2, and let UdU_{d} be a profinite group whose finite continuous quotients are precisely the finite perfect groups HH with d⁡(H)≤dd(H)\leq d. For every monolithic primitive finite group LL,

κL​(Ud)={fL​(d)−1,if L is perfect,0,otherwise.\kappa_{L}(U_{d})=\begin{cases}f_{L}(d)-1,&\text{if $L$ is perfect},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

If Ud=lim←n⁡PnU_{d}=\varprojlim_{n}P_{n} is an inverse limit of finite groups with surjective transition maps, then for each fixed LL there is an integer nLn_{L} such that

κL​(Pn)=κL​(Ud)(n≥nL).\kappa_{L}(P_{n})=\kappa_{L}(U_{d})\qquad(n\geq n_{L}).
Proof.

Put A=soc⁡(L)A=\soc(L). We first show that LtL_{t} is perfect if and only if LL is perfect. One implication follows from the projection Lt↠LL_{t}\twoheadrightarrow L. Conversely, suppose that LL is perfect. The subgroup AA cannot be central: Lemma 7.2 would give A≤Frat⁡(L)A\leq\Frat(L), contrary to primitivity. Minimal normality therefore gives [A,L]=A[A,L]=A. The projection of LtL_{t} onto each coordinate is surjective, so the commutators with each coordinate subgroup of AtA^{t} generate that subgroup. Thus At≤[Lt,Lt]A^{t}\leq[L_{t},L_{t}]. Since Lt/At≅L/AL_{t}/A^{t}\cong L/A is perfect, so is LtL_{t}.

If LL is not perfect, no LtL_{t} is a quotient of UdU_{d}, and hence κL​(Ud)=0\kappa_{L}(U_{d})=0. If LL is perfect, the defining property of UdU_{d} gives

Ud↠Lt⟺d(Lt)≤d⟺t<fL(d).U_{d}\twoheadrightarrow L_{t}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(L_{t})\leq d\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t<f_{L}(d).

This proves the formula, including the case fL​(d)=1f_{L}(d)=1.

Put k=κL​(Ud)k=\kappa_{L}(U_{d}). Each PnP_{n} is a quotient of UdU_{d}, so κL​(Pn)≤k\kappa_{L}(P_{n})\leq k. If k=0k=0, equality holds for every nn. If k>0k>0, an epimorphism Ud↠LkU_{d}\twoheadrightarrow L_{k} factors through some PnLP_{n_{L}}, and hence through every PnP_{n} with n≥nLn\geq n_{L}. Thus κL​(Pn)≥k\kappa_{L}(P_{n})\geq k for those nn, proving the assertion. ∎

7.2 Uniqueness

A topologically finitely generated profinite group is determined by its finite continuous quotients. We include a proof of this profinite form of the theorem of Dixon, Formanek, Poland, and Ribes [6].

Lemma 7.8.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a topologically finitely generated profinite group. Then every continuous epimorphism φ:𝒢↠𝒢\varphi:\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{G} is an isomorphism.

Proof.

Fix n≥1n\geq 1. A continuous action of 𝒢\mathcal{G} on {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\} is determined by the images of a finite topological generating set. Hence there are finitely many such actions. Every open subgroup of index nn is a point stabilizer of one of them, so the set 𝒰n\mathcal{U}_{n} of these subgroups is finite. Since φ\varphi is surjective, the map U↦φ−1​(U)U\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(U) is an injection from 𝒰n\mathcal{U}_{n} to itself and hence a bijection. Every open subgroup of index nn therefore contains ker⁡φ\ker\varphi. Since the open subgroups intersect in the identity, ker⁡φ=1\ker\varphi=1. Recall that for compact Hausdorff groups it suffices to show that a continuous homomorphism φ\varphi is bijective to grant that it is an isomorphism of topological groups. ∎

Proposition 7.9.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} and ℋ\mathcal{H} be topologically finitely generated profinite groups such that a finite group is a continuous quotient of 𝒢\mathcal{G} if and only if it is a continuous quotient of ℋ\mathcal{H}. Then 𝒢≅ℋ\mathcal{G}\cong\mathcal{H} as topological groups.

Proof.

For an open normal subgroup M​⊴​ℋM\trianglelefteq\mathcal{H}, put

SM=Sur⁡(𝒢,ℋ/M).S_{M}=\Sur(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{H}/M).

Each SMS_{M} is nonempty by hypothesis. It is finite because a continuous homomorphism to a finite group is determined by the images of a finite topological generating set. Postcomposition with the projections ℋ/M↠ℋ/M′\mathcal{H}/M\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{H}/M^{\prime} for M≤M′M\leq M^{\prime} makes (SM)M(S_{M})_{M} an inverse system of nonempty finite sets over the directed set of open normal subgroups of ℋ\mathcal{H}. Its inverse limit is nonempty by compactness. An element is a compatible family of epimorphisms, that is, a continuous homomorphism

φ:𝒢⟶lim←M⁡ℋ/M=ℋ\varphi:\mathcal{G}\longrightarrow\varprojlim_{M}\mathcal{H}/M=\mathcal{H}

whose image is dense. The image is compact and hence closed, so φ\varphi is surjective. The same argument gives a continuous epimorphism ψ:ℋ↠𝒢\psi:\mathcal{H}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{G}. The composite ψ∘φ:𝒢↠𝒢\psi\circ\varphi:\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{G} is an isomorphism by Lemma 7.8. Thus φ\varphi is injective and hence an isomorphism. ∎

Proof of Theorem 7.1(iii).

Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be as in (iii). Every finite continuous quotient QQ of 𝒱\mathcal{V} is dd-generated. Since 𝒱=[𝒱,𝒱]¯\mathcal{V}=\overline{[\mathcal{V},\mathcal{V}]}, its image in QQ is [Q,Q]¯=[Q,Q]\overline{[Q,Q]}=[Q,Q], so QQ is perfect. By hypothesis the finite continuous quotients of 𝒱\mathcal{V} also include every finite perfect dd-generated group. Hence 𝒱\mathcal{V} and UdU_{d} have the same finite continuous quotients, and Proposition 7.9 gives 𝒱≅Ud\mathcal{V}\cong U_{d}. ∎

7.3 Projectivity and presentations

A profinite group PP is projective if every continuous homomorphism P→BP\to B lifts through every continuous epimorphism A↠BA\twoheadrightarrow B of profinite groups.

Proposition 7.10.

Let d≥2d\geq 2. Every continuous epimorphism F^d↠Ud\widehat{F}_{d}\twoheadrightarrow U_{d} has a continuous section. In particular, UdU_{d} is projective.

Proof.

Fix an epimorphism π:F:=F^d↠Ud\pi:F:=\widehat{F}_{d}\twoheadrightarrow U_{d}. There is a closed subgroup P≤FP\leq F minimal among those mapping onto UdU_{d}. Indeed, the intersection of a descending chain of such subgroups still maps onto UdU_{d}: its intersection with each fibre of π\pi is nonempty by compactness. Zorn’s lemma therefore applies.

Choose a generating dd-tuple of UdU_{d} and lift it to PP. The closed subgroup generated by these lifts maps onto UdU_{d}, so it equals PP by minimality. Thus PP is topologically dd-generated. The closed subgroup [P,P]¯\overline{[P,P]} also maps onto UdU_{d}, since UdU_{d} is perfect. Minimality gives

P=[P,P]¯.P=\overline{[P,P]}.

Since PP maps onto UdU_{d}, its finite quotients include every finite perfect dd-generated group. Theorem 7.1(iii) gives an isomorphism j:Ud→Pj:U_{d}\to P. The composite π|P∘j\pi|_{P}\circ j is a surjective endomorphism of UdU_{d}, hence an isomorphism by Lemma 7.8. Therefore π|P\pi|_{P} is an isomorphism, and its inverse gives a continuous section s:Ud→Fs:U_{d}\to F.

To prove projectivity, let α:A↠B\alpha:A\twoheadrightarrow B and f:Ud→Bf:U_{d}\to B be continuous. Freeness gives a lift ℓ:F→A\ell:F\to A of f∘πf\circ\pi, by lifting the images of the free generators. Then ℓ∘s\ell\circ s lifts ff. ∎

Lemma 7.11.

Let F=F^dF=\widehat{F}_{d} have free generators x1,…,xdx_{1},\ldots,x_{d}, and let e:F→Fe:F\to F be a continuous endomorphism with e2=ee^{2}=e. Then

ker⁡e=⟨x1​e​(x1)−1,…,xd​e​(xd)−1⟩F¯.\ker e=\overline{\langle x_{1}e(x_{1})^{-1},\ldots,x_{d}e(x_{d})^{-1}\rangle^{F}}.
Proof.

Let RR be the closed normal subgroup on the right. Each of its stated generators lies in ker⁡e\ker e, so R≤ker⁡eR\leq\ker e. If q:F↠F/Rq:F\twoheadrightarrow F/R is the quotient map, then q=q∘eq=q\circ e on the free generators, and hence on FF. Thus qq kills ker⁡e\ker e, proving the reverse inclusion. ∎

Proposition 7.12.

Let d≥2d\geq 2. Then d⁡(Ud)=dd(U_{d})=d, and UdU_{d} admits a profinite presentation with dd generators and dd relators. Every profinite presentation of UdU_{d} has at least dd relators.

Proof.

We already know that d⁡(Ud)≤dd(U_{d})\leq d. For the reverse inequality, it suffices to find a finite perfect quotient of rank dd. For d=2d=2, take A5A_{5}. For d≥3d\geq 3, put t=fA5​(d−1)t=f_{A_{5}}(d-1). Appending an arbitrary element of A5A_{5} to a generating mm-tuple gives

|Genm+1⁡(A5)|≥60​|Genm⁡(A5)|>|Genm⁡(A5)|(m≥2).|\Gen_{m+1}(A_{5})|\geq 60|\Gen_{m}(A_{5})|>|\Gen_{m}(A_{5})|\qquad(m\geq 2).

By (9), this implies fA5​(d−1)<fA5​(d)f_{A_{5}}(d-1)<f_{A_{5}}(d). Hence

d−1<d⁡(A5t)≤d.d-1<d(A_{5}^{t})\leq d.

The finite perfect group A5tA_{5}^{t} is therefore a quotient of UdU_{d} of rank dd.

Choose an epimorphism π:F:=F^d↠Ud\pi:F:=\widehat{F}_{d}\twoheadrightarrow U_{d}. Proposition 7.10 gives a section s:Ud→Fs:U_{d}\to F. Then e=s∘πe=s\circ\pi is idempotent and ker⁡e=ker⁡π\ker e=\ker\pi. Lemma 7.11 gives the required dd relators.

For minimality, it suffices to consider finitely many relators. Suppose first that the presentation has n<∞n<\infty generators and relators y1,…,yk∈F^ny_{1},\ldots,y_{k}\in\widehat{F}_{n}. For any prime pp, let y¯i\bar{y}_{i} be their images in 𝔽pn\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}. Since UdU_{d} is perfect, passing to the maximal elementary abelian pp-quotient gives

0≅𝔽pn/⟨y¯1,…,y¯k⟩𝔽p,0\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}/\langle\bar{y}_{1},\ldots,\bar{y}_{k}\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{p}},

so k≥n≥d⁡(Ud)=dk\geq n\geq d(U_{d})=d. If the free source has infinitely many generators, it maps onto Cpk+1C_{p}^{k+1}. The images of the kk relators cannot span this quotient. The presented group then has a nontrivial elementary abelian quotient, so it cannot be UdU_{d}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 7.1(iv).

Combine Propositions 7.10 and 7.12. ∎

Remark 7.13.

The section in Proposition 7.10 identifies UdU_{d} with a closed subgroup of F^d\widehat{F}_{d}, and s∘πs\circ\pi is a retraction onto this subgroup.

Remark 7.14.

Theorem 7.1 proves the profinite Conjecture B1 of [25]. By Nikolov’s reductions, Conjecture A of [25] is therefore equivalent to Conjecture B2. The latter asks for a dense finitely generated abstractly perfect subgroup in every finitely generated perfect profinite group. Every topologically dd-generated perfect profinite group has all its finite continuous quotients among those of UdU_{d}. The compactness argument of Proposition 7.9 therefore makes it a continuous quotient of UdU_{d}. Dense finitely generated abstractly perfect subgroups pass to quotients. Thus Conjecture A is equivalent to the assertion that UdU_{d} contains such a subgroup for every d≥2d\geq 2.

8 Further applications

We apply the moment bounds to random groups with finite group actions and study positive finite generation in the Liu–Wood model.

8.1 A transfer principle for finite group actions

Let Γ\Gamma be a finite group. A profinite Γ\Gamma-group is a profinite group with a continuous action of Γ\Gamma by automorphisms. We write SurΓ⁡(X,A)\Sur_{\Gamma}(X,A) for the set of continuous epimorphisms ϕ:X→A\phi:X\to A such that ϕ⁡(γ⁡(x))=γ⁡(ϕ⁡(x))\phi(\gamma(x))=\gamma(\phi(x)) for all x∈Xx\in X and γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma. For Δ≤Γ\Delta\leq\Gamma, put

AΔ:={a∈A:γ⁡(a)=a​ for every ​γ∈Δ}.A^{\Delta}:=\{a\in A:\gamma(a)=a\text{ for every }\gamma\in\Delta\}.

The semidirect product X⋊ΓX\rtimes\Gamma has the product topology and multiplication

(x,γ)​(y,η)=(x​γ​(y),γ​η).(x,\gamma)(y,\eta)=(x\gamma(y),\gamma\eta).

Let Π\Pi be a set of primes not dividing |Γ||\Gamma|. A finite Π\Pi-group is a finite group whose order has all its prime divisors in Π\Pi. A profinite group is pro-Π\Pi if every finite continuous quotient is a Π\Pi-group. We also write pro-m′m^{\prime} when Π\Pi consists of the primes not dividing mm. A pro-Π\Pi Γ\Gamma-group XX is admissible if

X=⟨x−1γ(x):x∈X,γ∈Γ⟩¯.X=\overline{\langle x^{-1}\gamma(x):x\in X,\ \gamma\in\Gamma\rangle}.

For a finite group QQ, let OΠ​(Q)O_{\Pi}(Q) be its largest normal Π\Pi-subgroup.

Proposition 8.1.

Let XX be a random admissible pro-Π\Pi Γ\Gamma-group. Suppose that the functions |SurΓ⁡(X,A)||\Sur_{\Gamma}(X,A)| are measurable and that, for some M≥1M\geq 1 and β≥0\beta\geq 0,

𝔼​|SurΓ⁡(X,A)|≤M​|A|β\mathbb{E}|\Sur_{\Gamma}(X,A)|\leq M|A|^{\beta} (51)

for every finite admissible Π\Pi-Γ\Gamma-group AA. Then, for every finite group QQ,

𝔼​|Sur⁡(X⋊Γ,Q)|≤M​|Q|d⁡(Γ)+β.\mathbb{E}|\Sur(X\rtimes\Gamma,Q)|\leq M|Q|^{d(\Gamma)+\beta}. (52)

Both X⋊ΓX\rtimes\Gamma and XX are topologically finitely generated almost surely.

Proof.

Put Y=X⋊ΓY=X\rtimes\Gamma. If f:Y↠Qf:Y\twoheadrightarrow Q and N=f⁡(X)N=f(X), then NN is a normal Π\Pi-subgroup and Q/NQ/N is a quotient of Γ\Gamma. Every normal Π\Pi-subgroup of QQ maps trivially to Q/NQ/N, since its image has order dividing |Γ||\Gamma| and has all its prime divisors in Π\Pi. Hence N=OΠ​(Q)N=O_{\Pi}(Q).

Let ρ=f|Γ\rho=f|_{\Gamma}. The restriction f|Xf|_{X} is a Γ\Gamma-equivariant epimorphism onto OΠ​(Q)O_{\Pi}(Q) for the action

γ⋅a=ρ⁡(γ)​a​ρ​(γ)−1.\gamma\cdot a=\rho(\gamma)a\rho(\gamma)^{-1}.

Denote this Γ\Gamma-group by OΠ​(Q)ρO_{\Pi}(Q)_{\rho}. Conversely, if ρ:Γ→Q\rho:\Gamma\to Q satisfies Q=OΠ​(Q)​ρ​(Γ)Q=O_{\Pi}(Q)\rho(\Gamma) and ϕ:X↠OΠ​(Q)ρ\phi:X\twoheadrightarrow O_{\Pi}(Q)_{\rho} is equivariant, then

(x,γ)⟼ϕ⁡(x)​ρ​(γ)(x,\gamma)\longmapsto\phi(x)\rho(\gamma)

is an epimorphism Y↠QY\twoheadrightarrow Q. Thus

|Sur⁡(Y,Q)|=∑ρ∈Hom⁡(Γ,Q)Q=OΠ​(Q)​ρ​(Γ)|SurΓ⁡(X,OΠ​(Q)ρ)|.|\Sur(Y,Q)|=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\in\Hom(\Gamma,Q)\\ Q=O_{\Pi}(Q)\rho(\Gamma)\end{subarray}}|\Sur_{\Gamma}(X,O_{\Pi}(Q)_{\rho})|. (53)

Every equivariant quotient of XX is admissible. A summand in (53) is therefore zero unless its target is admissible. In the remaining cases, (51) applies. Since

|Hom⁡(Γ,Q)|≤|Q|d⁡(Γ),|OΠ​(Q)|≤|Q|,|\Hom(\Gamma,Q)|\leq|Q|^{d(\Gamma)},\qquad|O_{\Pi}(Q)|\leq|Q|,

taking expectations gives (52). The finite sum also proves measurability. Theorem 1.1, with δ=0\delta=0, shows that YY is finitely generated almost surely. The profinite Schreier bound [27, Section 3.6] gives

d(X)≤1+[Y:X](d(Y)−1)=1+|Γ|(d(Y)−1),d(X)\leq 1+[Y:X](d(Y)-1)=1+|\Gamma|(d(Y)-1),

so XX is finitely generated almost surely. ∎

We apply this proposition to three probability measures defined by random presentations. We write μΓ,u\mu_{\Gamma,u} for the measure constructed by Liu–Wood–Zureick-Brown in [23, Definition 3.15 and Section 5.4], μΓ,Γ∞\mu_{\Gamma,\Gamma_{\infty}} for the measure constructed by Liu–Willyard in [21, Definition 6.1], and μ𝚪\mu_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}} for the measure constructed by Willyard in [32, Definitions 5.1, 5.2, and 5.5]. Here u∈ℤu\in\mathbb{Z} in the first case, Γ∞≤Γ\Gamma_{\infty}\leq\Gamma is cyclic in the second, and 𝚪=(Γ1,…,Γu+1)\boldsymbol{\Gamma}=(\Gamma_{1},\ldots,\Gamma_{u+1}), with u≥0u\geq 0 and Γi≤Γ\Gamma_{i}\leq\Gamma, in the third. The underlying spaces and their topologies are defined in [23, Section 3.2], [21, Section 6], and [32, Section 5], respectively. Their basic open sets specify the isomorphism type of the maximal quotient in the class generated by a finite set of finite Γ\Gamma-groups under Γ\Gamma-invariant subgroups, Γ\Gamma-equivariant quotients, and finite products. The functions |SurΓ⁡(X,A)||\Sur_{\Gamma}(X,A)| are constant on such basic open sets once the chosen class contains AA, and hence are measurable.

Corollary 8.2.

The following random profinite Γ\Gamma-groups are topologically finitely generated almost surely.

  1. (i)

    The Liu–Wood–Zureick-Brown law μΓ,u\mu_{\Gamma,u}, for u∈ℤu\in\mathbb{Z}.

  2. (ii)

    The Liu–Willyard law μΓ,Γ∞\mu_{\Gamma,\Gamma_{\infty}}, where Γ∞≤Γ\Gamma_{\infty}\leq\Gamma is cyclic.

  3. (iii)

    Willyard’s law μ𝚪\mu_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}, where 𝚪=(Γ1,…,Γu+1)\boldsymbol{\Gamma}=(\Gamma_{1},\ldots,\Gamma_{u+1}), u≥0u\geq 0, and Γi≤Γ\Gamma_{i}\leq\Gamma.

If XX has the respective law, then for every finite group QQ,

𝔼​|Sur⁡(X⋊Γ,Q)|≤{|Q|d⁡(Γ)+max⁡{0,−u}in (i),|Q|d⁡(Γ)in (ii) and (iii).\mathbb{E}|\Sur(X\rtimes\Gamma,Q)|\leq\begin{cases}|Q|^{d(\Gamma)+\max\{0,-u\}}&\text{in {(i)}},\\ |Q|^{d(\Gamma)}&\text{in {(ii)} and {(iii)}}.\end{cases}
Proof.

These laws are supported on admissible pro-|Γ|′|\Gamma|^{\prime} groups in (i) and (iii), and on admissible pro-(2​|Γ|)′(2|\Gamma|)^{\prime} groups in (ii). For each finite admissible target AA in the corresponding category, the cited papers prove

𝔼μΓ,u​|SurΓ⁡(X,A)|\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\Gamma,u}}|\Sur_{\Gamma}(X,A)| =[A:AΓ]−u≤|A|max⁡{0,−u},\displaystyle=[A:A^{\Gamma}]^{-u}\leq|A|^{\max\{0,-u\}}, (54)
𝔼μΓ,Γ∞​|SurΓ⁡(X,A)|\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\Gamma,\Gamma_{\infty}}}|\Sur_{\Gamma}(X,A)| =[AΓ∞:AΓ]−1≤1,\displaystyle=[A^{\Gamma_{\infty}}:A^{\Gamma}]^{-1}\leq 1, (55)
𝔼μ𝚪​|SurΓ⁡(X,A)|\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}}|\Sur_{\Gamma}(X,A)| =|AΓ|∏i=1u+1|AΓi|≤|AΓ|−u≤1.\displaystyle=\frac{|A^{\Gamma}|}{\prod_{i=1}^{u+1}|A^{\Gamma_{i}}|}\leq|A^{\Gamma}|^{-u}\leq 1. (56)

These are [23, Theorem 6.2], [21, Theorem 6.3(3)], and [32, Theorem 6.2], respectively. The last inequality uses AΓ≤AΓiA^{\Gamma}\leq A^{\Gamma_{i}} for each ii. Proposition 8.1 gives the assertions. ∎

The corollary concerns the probability measures defined by these random presentations. Their conjectural relation to Galois groups is described in the cited papers.

8.2 Positive finite generation

For a profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, let μ𝒢\mu_{\mathcal{G}} be its normalized Haar measure, the translation-invariant Borel probability measure on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Put

P⁡(𝒢,d):=μ𝒢⊗d​{(g1,…,gd):⟨g1,…,gd⟩¯=𝒢}.P(\mathcal{G},d):=\mu_{\mathcal{G}}^{\otimes d}\{(g_{1},\ldots,g_{d}):\overline{\langle g_{1},\ldots,g_{d}\rangle}=\mathcal{G}\}.

The group 𝒢\mathcal{G} is positively finitely generated, or PFG, if P⁡(𝒢,d)>0P(\mathcal{G},d)>0 for some integer d≥1d\geq 1. It has polynomial maximal-subgroup growth if the number of maximal open subgroups of index nn is at most ncn^{c} for some fixed cc and every n≥2n\geq 2. These properties are equivalent by [24, Theorem 4].

A closed normal subgroup N​⊴​HN\trianglelefteq H is positively finitely normally generated in HH if, for some k≥1k\geq 1,

μN⊗k​{(x1,…,xk):⟨x1,…,xk⟩H¯=N}>0.\mu_{N}^{\otimes k}\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}):\overline{\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\rangle^{H}}=N\}>0.

Here ⟨x1,…,xk⟩H¯\overline{\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\rangle^{H}} is the smallest closed normal subgroup of HH containing the tuple. A finitely generated profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G} is positively finitely related, or PFR, if this condition holds for the kernel of every continuous epimorphism H↠𝒢H\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{G} with HH finitely generated [14, Definition 3.3 and Lemma 3.4].

For a prime pp and n≥1n\geq 1, let rn​(𝒢,p)r_{n}(\mathcal{G},p) count the isomorphism classes of continuous irreducible representations 𝒢→GLn⁡(𝔽p)\mathcal{G}\to\GL_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}). Irreducibility means that the only invariant subspaces are 00 and 𝔽pn\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}; isomorphism means conjugacy by GLn⁡(𝔽p)\GL_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}). The group 𝒢\mathcal{G} has uniformly bounded exponential representation growth, or UBERG, if

rn​(𝒢,p)≤pc​nr_{n}(\mathcal{G},p)\leq p^{cn}

for some cc independent of pp and nn [14, Definition 5.1].

A minimal extension of a finitely generated profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a continuous epimorphism π:E↠𝒢\pi:E\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{G}, with EE profinite, whose kernel is a finite nontrivial minimal normal subgroup of EE. Its degree is |ker⁡π||\ker\pi|. We count extensions up to continuous isomorphisms commuting with their maps to 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The group 𝒢\mathcal{G} has polynomial minimal-extension growth if there is a constant cc such that the number of these isomorphism classes of degree nn is at most ncn^{c} for every n≥2n\geq 2 [14, Section 3.4].

A profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G} is positively finitely presented if it is PFG and the kernel of every epimorphism P↠𝒢P\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{G} from a PFG projective profinite group is positively finitely normally generated in PP. Projectivity is defined in Section 7. Equivalently, 𝒢\mathcal{G} is PFG and finitely presented [3, Definition 3.2 and Proposition 3.3].

We use the following criterion of Jaikin-Zapirain and Pyber. Let LL be a finite monolithic primitive group with nonabelian socle AA. Recall its crown multiplicity

κL​(𝒢):=sup{k≥1:𝒢↠Lk},\kappa_{L}(\mathcal{G}):=\sup\{k\geq 1:\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow L_{k}\}, (57)

where the supremum of the empty set is 00. Write l⁡(A)l(A) for the least degree of a faithful transitive permutation representation of AA. Thus l⁡(A)l(A) is the least cardinality of a finite set on which AA acts transitively with trivial kernel. A transitive permutation action is primitive if it preserves no partition other than the partition into singletons and the partition with one part.

A finitely generated profinite group 𝒢\mathcal{G} is PFG if and only if there is a constant cc such that

κL​(𝒢)≤l​(A)c\kappa_{L}(\mathcal{G})\leq l(A)^{c} (58)

for every finite monolithic primitive group LL with nonabelian socle AA. An equivalent condition is that, for some cc,

|Sur⁡(𝒢,L)|≤|L|​l​(A)c|\Sur(\mathcal{G},L)|\leq|L|\,l(A)^{c} (59)

for every such LL [13, Theorem 11.1].

The properties used below define Borel sets on the locus of finitely generated groups. Indeed, this locus is Borel by Section 2, and (59) expresses PFG using countably many inequalities between continuous epimorphism-counting functions. For fixed p,np,n, the function rn​(𝒢,p)r_{n}(\mathcal{G},p) depends only on the level-{GLn⁡(𝔽p)}\{\GL_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\} completion, so it is continuous. Taking the union over integral c≥1c\geq 1 in the definition of UBERG shows that its locus is Borel. Finally, PFR and polynomial minimal-extension growth are equivalent to finite presentation together with UBERG on this locus [14, Theorems 3.9 and 5.6]. Proposition 5.2 and the characterization of positive finite presentation above give the remaining assertions.

Lemma 8.3.

For each integer D≥1D\geq 1, there is a constant CDC_{D} such that, for every integer n≥2n\geq 2, at most nCDn^{C_{D}} isomorphism classes of finite monolithic primitive groups LL satisfy

d⁡(L)≤D,A=soc⁡(L)​ is nonabelian,l⁡(A)=n.d(L)\leq D,\qquad A=\soc(L)\text{ is nonabelian},\qquad l(A)=n.
Proof.

By [13, Lemma 9.2], each such LL has a faithful primitive permutation representation of degree at most nc7n^{c_{7}}, for an absolute constant c7c_{7}. By [13, Theorem 8.1], there are at most mcp​Dm^{c_{p}D} conjugacy classes of DD-generated primitive subgroups of Sym⁡(m)\Sym(m), for an absolute constant cpc_{p}. Thus the number in question is at most

∑m≤nc7mcp​D≤nc7​(cp​D+1).\sum_{m\leq n^{c_{7}}}m^{c_{p}D}\leq n^{c_{7}(c_{p}D+1)}. (60)

We may take CD=c7​(cp​D+1)C_{D}=c_{7}(c_{p}D+1). ∎

For a nonabelian finite simple group SS, the quantity QS​(𝒢)Q_{S}(\mathcal{G}) from (37) counts the open normal subgroups with quotient isomorphic to SS. Distinct such kernels give an epimorphism onto the product of the quotients. Hence

κS​(𝒢)=QS​(𝒢).\kappa_{S}(\mathcal{G})=Q_{S}(\mathcal{G}). (61)

Lemma 5.7 gives their joint distribution under μu\mu_{u}.

Theorem 8.4.

Let u∈ℤu\in\mathbb{Z}, and let 𝒢\mathcal{G} have law μu\mu_{u}.

  1. (i)

    If u≥0u\geq 0, then almost surely

    supLκL​(𝒢)<∞,\sup_{L}\kappa_{L}(\mathcal{G})<\infty, (62)

    where LL ranges over the finite monolithic primitive groups with nonabelian socle.

  2. (ii)

    If u=−1u=-1, then 𝒢\mathcal{G} is PFG almost surely, but

    supLκL​(𝒢)=∞\sup_{L}\kappa_{L}(\mathcal{G})=\infty (63)

    almost surely. For every k≥1k\geq 1, infinitely many alternating simple groups AnA_{n} satisfy 𝒢↠Ank\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow A_{n}^{k}, almost surely.

  3. (iii)

    If u≤−2u\leq-2, then 𝒢\mathcal{G} is not PFG and does not have UBERG, almost surely.

Consequently,

μu​{𝒢:𝒢​ is PFG}={1,u≥−1,0,u≤−2.\mu_{u}\{\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{G}\text{ is PFG}\}=\begin{cases}1,&u\geq-1,\\ 0,&u\leq-2.\end{cases} (64)

In the range u≥−1u\geq-1, almost every 𝒢\mathcal{G} is PFR, has polynomial minimal-extension growth, has UBERG, and is positively finitely presented. In the range u≤−2u\leq-2, almost every 𝒢\mathcal{G} has none of these properties.

Proof.

Suppose first that u≥0u\geq 0, and fix D≥1D\geq 1. Let LL be monolithic primitive with nonabelian socle AA, and put K=L/AK=L/A and n=l⁡(A)n=l(A). The action of AA on itself by left multiplication gives n≤|A|n\leq|A|. Since |Lk|=|K|​|A|k|L_{k}|=|K||A|^{k}, Proposition 4.1(ii) and the Liu–Wood moment identity give

μu​{𝒢:𝒢↠Lk}≤|Lk|−u|Aut⁡(Lk)|≤|K|−u​|A|−(u+1)​kk!≤n−(u+1)​k.\mu_{u}\{\mathcal{G}:\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow L_{k}\}\leq\frac{|L_{k}|^{-u}}{|\Aut(L_{k})|}\leq\frac{|K|^{-u}|A|^{-(u+1)k}}{k!}\leq n^{-(u+1)k}. (65)

Let ED,kE_{D,k} be the event that d⁡(𝒢)≤Dd(\mathcal{G})\leq D and 𝒢\mathcal{G} has a quotient LkL_{k} with soc⁡(L)\soc(L) nonabelian. Every such LL is DD-generated. Lemma 8.3 therefore gives

μu​(ED,k)≤∑n≥2nCD−(u+1)​k.\mu_{u}(E_{D,k})\leq\sum_{n\geq 2}n^{C_{D}-(u+1)k}. (66)

For sufficiently large kk, the summands are bounded by n−2n^{-2} and tend to zero termwise as k→∞k\to\infty. Hence the right-hand side tends to zero by dominated convergence. The events ED,kE_{D,k} decrease, with intersection

{d(𝒢)≤D,supLκL(𝒢)=∞}.\{d(\mathcal{G})\leq D,\ \sup_{L}\kappa_{L}(\mathcal{G})=\infty\}.

This intersection has measure zero. Almost-sure finite generation and a union over DD prove (i).

We next prove that 𝒢\mathcal{G} is PFG almost surely for every u≥−1u\geq-1. Fix D≥1D\geq 1, and choose an integer a>CD+1a>C_{D}+1. For each DD-generated monolithic primitive group LL with nonabelian socle AA, set n=l⁡(A)n=l(A) and

BL​(a):={𝒢:|Sur⁡(𝒢,L)|>|L|​na}.B_{L}(a):=\{\mathcal{G}:|\Sur(\mathcal{G},L)|>|L|n^{a}\}.

Markov’s inequality gives

μu​(BL​(a))≤|L|−u−1​n−a≤n−a.\mu_{u}(B_{L}(a))\leq|L|^{-u-1}n^{-a}\leq n^{-a}. (67)

By Lemma 8.3,

∑L​ monolithic primitivesoc⁡(L)​ nonabelian,d⁡(L)≤Dμu​(BL​(a))≤∑n≥2nCD−a<∞.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}L\text{ monolithic primitive}\\ \soc(L)\text{ nonabelian},\ d(L)\leq D\end{subarray}}\mu_{u}(B_{L}(a))\leq\sum_{n\geq 2}n^{C_{D}-a}<\infty.

The first Borel–Cantelli lemma shows that, almost surely, only finitely many of these LL violate (59) with exponent aa. On the event d⁡(𝒢)≤Dd(\mathcal{G})\leq D, all epimorphism counts are finite. The finitely many exceptions can therefore be included by increasing aa to a finite value depending on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. A group LL with d⁡(L)>Dd(L)>D is not a quotient of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, so its epimorphism count is zero. Thus (59) holds for every relevant LL. Almost-sure finite generation and a union over DD prove the assertion.

When u=−1u=-1, Lemma 5.7 gives independent random variables

QAn∼Pois⁡(1/2)(n≥7),Q_{A_{n}}\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1/2)\qquad(n\geq 7),

since |Out⁡(An)|=2|\Out(A_{n})|=2. For each fixed k≥1k\geq 1, the events QAn≥kQ_{A_{n}}\geq k are independent and have the same positive probability. By the second Borel–Cantelli lemma, infinitely many of them occur, almost surely. Intersecting over kk and using (61) proves (ii).

Suppose now that u≤−2u\leq-2. For m≥5m\geq 5, put

Tm:=PSLm​(2)=GLm⁡(2).T_{m}:=\mathrm{PSL}_{m}(2)=\GL_{m}(2).

These are pairwise nonisomorphic finite simple groups with |Out⁡(Tm)|≤2|\Out(T_{m})|\leq 2 [2], and

|Tm|=2m2​∏j=1m(1−2−j)≥η2​(∞)​2m2.|T_{m}|=2^{m^{2}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}(1-2^{-j})\geq\eta_{2}(\infty)2^{m^{2}}. (68)

The Poisson mean in (39) consequently satisfies

λTm,u=|Tm|−u−1|Out⁡(Tm)|≥η2​(∞)2​ 2m2.\lambda_{T_{m},u}=\frac{|T_{m}|^{-u-1}}{|\Out(T_{m})|}\geq\frac{\eta_{2}(\infty)}{2}\,2^{m^{2}}. (69)

Fix c≥1c\geq 1. For all sufficiently large mm, 2c​m≤λTm,u/22^{cm}\leq\lambda_{T_{m},u}/2. Applying Markov’s inequality to 2−QTm2^{-Q_{T_{m}}} gives

μu{QTm≤2c​m}≤μu{QTm≤λTm,u/2}≤exp(−λTm,u/8).\mu_{u}\{Q_{T_{m}}\leq 2^{cm}\}\leq\mu_{u}\{Q_{T_{m}}\leq\lambda_{T_{m},u}/2\}\leq\exp(-\lambda_{T_{m},u}/8). (70)

The right-hand side is summable in mm. Hence, almost surely,

QTm​(𝒢)>2c​mQ_{T_{m}}(\mathcal{G})>2^{cm} (71)

for all sufficiently large mm. Intersecting over integral cc makes this simultaneous for every fixed cc.

The natural action of Tm=GLm⁡(2)T_{m}=\GL_{m}(2) on the nonzero vectors of 𝔽2m\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m} is faithful and transitive, and hence

l⁡(Tm)≤2m−1.l(T_{m})\leq 2^{m}-1.

Together with (61), (71) violates (58) for every exponent. Thus 𝒢\mathcal{G} is not PFG.

The same groups prove failure of UBERG. The natural representation of Tm=GLm⁡(2)T_{m}=\GL_{m}(2) on 𝔽2m\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m} is faithful and irreducible. Choose one epimorphism 𝒢↠Tm\mathcal{G}\twoheadrightarrow T_{m} for each kernel counted by QTm​(𝒢)Q_{T_{m}}(\mathcal{G}), and compose it with this representation. The resulting representations have distinct kernels and hence are pairwise nonisomorphic. Thus

rm​(𝒢,2)≥QTm​(𝒢).r_{m}(\mathcal{G},2)\geq Q_{T_{m}}(\mathcal{G}).

Equation (71) contradicts every bound rm​(𝒢,2)≤2c​mr_{m}(\mathcal{G},2)\leq 2^{cm}, so 𝒢\mathcal{G} does not have UBERG.

By Theorem 1.3, 𝒢\mathcal{G} is finitely presented almost surely. PFR is equivalent to polynomial minimal-extension growth, and for finitely presented groups it is also equivalent to UBERG [14, Theorems 3.9 and 5.6]. PFG implies UBERG [3, Corollary 1.11]. Together with the characterization of positive finite presentation above, these implications prove the remaining assertions.

∎

Theorem 8.4 implies in particular Theorem 1.6.
